On the motion of Sir Robert Borden for Committee of Supply:
Mr. E. LAPOINTE (Kamouraska) moved in amendment, seconded by Mr. E. B. Devlin:
That all the words after " that " in the main motion toe struck out and the following substituted therefor:
" It has long been the fettled policy of Great Britain whenever a country passed under the sovereignty of the Crown by treaty or otherwise, to respect the religion, usages and language of the inhabitants who thus become British subjects:
"That His Majesty's subjects of French origin in the province of Ontario complain that by recent legislation they have been to a large extent deprived of the privilege which they and their fathers have always enjoyed since Canada passed under the sovereignty of the British Crown, of having their children taught in French.
" That this House especially at this time of universal sacrifice and anxiety, when all energies should toe concentrated on the winning of the war, would, while fully recognizing the principle of provincial rights and the necessity of every child being given a thorough English education, respectfully suggest to the Legislative Assembly the wisdom of making it clear that the privilege of the children of French parentage of being taught in their mother tongue be not interfered with."

Whatever may be said about the point of order, which will be within your disposition, Mr. Speaker, and as to which it might be well for you to take time to make your ruling, I would suggest to my hon. friend who proposes this motion that, whether the point of order be well taken or not, he is bringing into this House a subject over which this House has no jurisdiction, and that, therefore, he ought most carefully to consider whether he is well advised in introducing it here. There is no question that a certain feeling has been aroused in different parts of the country-it is not confined to one part of the country-with respect to matters that are the subject of provincial jurisdiction; and I desire to appeal most earnestly to the hon. gentleman who proposes to introduce this resolution that he should not proceed with it. Its terms, perhaps, I did not accurately gather. A proposed resolution was handed to me last evening by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, but after listening to the resolution which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lapointe) proposes, I find that it differs somewhat from that which I received from my right hon. friend. In any event, it seems to me that, if my hon. friend is determined to precipitate a debate, which, so far as I see, can do no possible good, and which, in my judgment, may do an infinite amount of harm, the exact terms of the proposed resolution ought to be submitted for the information of the House before any debate takes place. Therefore it would be well, in order that His Honour the Speaker should have an opportunity of considering tne point of order which has been raised, and also that my hon. friend who proposes to move this resolution may have the opportunity for more careful and weighty reflection and consideration, that this motion should stand until to-morrow. In
the meantime His Honour the Speaker may take into consideration the point of order which has been raised by the hon. member for Moosejaw.

Mr. Speaker,
I beg to submit, in all humility, but with great force, that the point of order of my hon. friend from Moosejaw is not at all well taken. There is an abundance of precedents in this very House against it. As to the legislation of the province of Ontario which it is proposed to discuss to-day, m no hostile spirit, I am sure, we have the precedents in this House, in the time of Sir John Macdonald, in the time of Liberal <md Conservative Administrations, of resolutions in favour of Home Rule being presented and adopted, not once, not twice, but three times, and perhaps four, within my recollection. I have to say also that upon more than one occasion the British Parliament was moved, amongst others by Mr. Gladstone, to consider the treatment of Christian populations in the 'Orient. If I had supposed that any question would be raised as to the power of this House to consider or pass such a resolution, I could have armed myself with any number of precedents. As to the wisdom, or otherwise, of this motion, may I say to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that for my part I have another and a totally different view from the one which he has expressed. Everybody knows that there is in this province at the present time a widespread agitation with regard to the rights of the French language in this Dominion. It is never a wise thing to run away from a question.
Hear, hear.

I do not want any applause. I address myself to the common sense and the spirit of fairness of my fellow countrymen in the province of Ontario, and I repeat that we have nothing to gain by running away from the question. Let us discuss it like men; let us discuss it like the British subjects that we are. I speak here as a member of the minority; but no one is prouder of his British rights than I am myself, and I can appeal to my forty years in this House to justify what I now say. There is nothing to be gained by running away from this question. Let us discuss it; let us hear both sides of it; and then, Sir, I believe that from this discussion we shall rise wiser and better men, knowing better what our position is, knowing better what the rights of the minority

are; and I venture to say that when the question has been settled, as it ought to be settled, the minority will accept the situation whatever it may be.

Mr. Speaker, just a word upon the question of order raised by my hon. friend from Moosejaw. I do not think the precedents which have been advanced by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition have any application. The precedents that he has referred to are the precedents of Home Rule resolutions, which on several occasions were moved in this House, and also certain resolutions which were moved in the House of Commons in England with reference to the Christian populations of the Orient. I do not think that any benefit can be derived from the first precedent, that is, the passage of Home Rule resolutions by this House. I have not seen the terms of the present resolution, but, if I am correctly informed, we are asked to comment to a certain degree upon the action of a legislature in this Dominion. The powers conferred upon the legislature and upon the Dominion are defined very clearly by the British North America Act, and it seems to me that, by reason of that clear definition, any interference by this House in a question which concerns a legislature is an interference which cannot be justified by saying that upon another occasion the House expressed itself in favour of Home Rule. Let me call the attention of the House to the fact that the resolutions which were passed in favour of Home Rule were addressed to His Majesty's Government, and did not have the same significance as a resolution in this Federal House approving or blaming a legislature in the Dominion. Let me say one word to my hon. friend1 from Kamour-aska (Mr. E. Lapointe) who has- moved this resolution. I am as much concerned over this question as my hon. friend. I take as much interest, and have taken as much, interest in it from the very first time that it was mentioned, as my hon. friend, and more than my hon. friend has done while he ha6 been a member of this House. I have not had occasion to see the motion. I was unavoidably kept away from the House last evening. I saw a form of resolution this morning, but I am told that that is not th'e resolution which .is before the House. I suppose that what my hon. friend has in mind is the good of the cause which he

is advocating. If it is, and if he really does want an intelligent and clear discussion of the question, let him give notice of the resolution which he intends to move, so that we may see what attitude we upon this side of the House, or amongst ourselves, will take upon it; or, let him at least give us time to prepare any argument which he thinks we should bring forward either in favour of the resolution or against it.

May I ask that if hon. gentlemen want to have until to-morrow, or another day, to examine the resolution which is presented, I certainly would advise my hon. friend (Mir. Lapointe) to agree at once to the suggestion.

Public Works-harbours and rivers, New-Brunswick-Kouchibouguae, $10,500.

['Yes, $20,000 a mile. There was a railroad built by the city of Winnipeg from Winnipeg east within the last couple of years, and the only difference between the construction of that road and the construction of the branch lines on the prairie by the Canadian Northern is that the rails are somewhat lighter. They have a 60-pound rail, and in some cases the branch lines may have rails over 60 pounds. That road was built and equipped, as far as was necessary, for $12,000 a mile, or about half of what is charged up on the Canadian Northern, proving what I say that the money that this Government and the local Governments have advanced, as well as the proceeds of securities not guaranteed by either, has been switched from the Canadian Northern altogether, and put into concerns in Mexico, Toronto and elsewhere, and has gone into the pockets of the promoters of these enterprises. Now they come forward, and they do not put up one cent of their money. They did not put up anything two years ago when they came and asked for a guarantee. The Government gave that guarantee, and took no precautions to see that the money all went into the road, and now the company comes forward again and says: You must give us more money or we will throw the road on your hands. They came and held the Government up, and now the Government says: Well, we will give you $15,000,000 more and pay $3,000,000 of interest. That is the position of affairs to-day, and next year it will be just as bad, and perhaps worse. What are you going to do about it? Why not face the music like men? The war is not going to be over next year; certainly our war expenditure will not be over, and what better position can we expect to be in? We will have $300,000,000 or perhaps $400,000,000 more of debt than we have to-day, and we will be', "in a worse position to deal with this question. It is a most serious matter. Inside of five years Canada will have from one and a half billions to two billion dollars of debt to face. These two railroads will have to be looked after in some way, and if the Government takes them over, or keeps on fathering them, we will be liable for the whole business; and we will have from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000 of fixed charges and interest to pay every year. The situation will be worse if you let Mackenzie & Mann handle the Canadian Northern. If you are going to give them the money, why not give it iri such a manner that you will have some control. I do not like the idea of Government ownership; I have no use for it if it can be avoided; but there may be a worse thing than Government ownership. According to my idea, -it is a worse thing to pour money in and let somebody else handle it just as it suits him while you take the liability, and while you are not sure that all the money goes into the road. That is the position we are in to-day, and I think the Government ought to reconsider their attitude in regard to the matter. There might be some excuse for going to the rescue of these two roads because the Dominion and the provinces have so much in them, but what excuse is there for voting millions, either money or guaranteed bonds, to take over two roads in Quebec and to add to the Intercolonial that is losing money every year, simply to help out a political friend at a time when Canada cannot afford to put $1,000,000, or $4,000,000, in cash or securities into these roads? It is bad enough to help out the roads that the Government has some liability for, but to shoulder new liabilities where the Government has no responsibility whatever is one of the most criminal things that a government could do considering the financial position that Canada is in to-day.

What is to be done here?

This amount of $10,500 is asked for by District Engineer Stead for repairs and improvements to the harbour-at Kouchibouguac, which was badly damaged by a storm on 20th November, 1914. The proposed works will consist of the con-

struetion of a new dam, the repairing and extension of the old dam, and the rebuilding of pile breastworks. The estimated cost is as follows: dam to close new opening in beach, 800 feet long, at $0 per foot, $7,200; pile breastworks repaired and rebuilt, 1,000 feet, at $1.50, $1,500; extending old dam, 200 .feet, at $4, $800; repairing dam, 125 feet; and contingencies, $1,000.

I heartily agree with
what the minister proposes to do at Kouchi-bouguac. The storm caused very serious damage, and I hope the minister will see that the new work is done very thoroughly, so that the breakwater will not be carried away by the next bad storm.

If the minister would
permit me on this item, I should like to remind him that on Friday last, I think, I asked him to lay on the Table a copy of the fair-wage clause in regard to the work to be done at the Parliament Buildings. The minister's answer was that the committee would meet the next day. Of course, I did not understand that that committee which was to meet next day had anything to do with the fair wage clause in connection with that work; I assumed that that belonged to the Labour Department, and, I suppose, to the Minister of Public Works. It seems to me that it should be laid on the table for a good many reasons. My information is that the wages -of some of the workmen on the building have been lowered since last winter, notwithstanding that we hear it stated in Parliament every day that the cost of living is increasing. I do not know how this work is to be carried on, whether by contract, or on a percentage, or in. any other way; but that makes no real difference, the Government of Canada ought to pay at least as much as any private contractor in the city of Ottawa is called upon to pay. And it seems to me it would be much better in the interests of labour in this country that we should know as soon, as possible the wages that the workers may expect to receive in this work of rebuilding. I have just said that wages were lower. My information comes directly from the men working on the building. Last winter the carpenters received 40 cents an hour, but now they are paid 35 cents an hour. I believe that 35 cents an. hour was the rate provided for in the fair wage clause applied to the custom house building. But the contract for that was made six years ago, and conditions have greatly changed since that time-the Minister of Public Works knows

that as well as I do. Therefore, it would not be fair to suppose that the same rate would apply to the present work as applied to the construction of the custom house. Furthermore, in the case of the custom house contract, provision, was made for an eight-hour day. As the work of rebuilding the Pafliament buildings is supposed to go on with rapidity, it may be found necessary to have three .shifts a day. In that case it will be much better for the contractor, and for the Government as well, that an eight-hour day should be provided. -
If	you	have a	nine-hour day,	youcannot	have mo-re	than two .shifts,	andyou	are liable,	not infrequently,	tobe	in	such a	position as- to	be
compelled to use overtime; whereas, if you have three shifts, no overtime has to be paid. Of course, the wages should be in proportion to the cost of living. The Minister of Labour knows that according to the report of his department a family cannot live honestly on much less than $900 a year. The total of items contained in his report is about $800, but there are many items omitted which simply must be paid for by every family. I bring this matter up now because I suppose arrangements for the work are not yet completed, and it is well to provide in such a way as to give satisfaction to those interested in the work. I have spoken specially of the carpenters, but I might refer to those in other trades. I trust the Minister of Labour will consult the representatives of the different trades in Ottawa, and will get the report of his fair wage officers on this .subject. I think he will find that the wages are, in some cases, far below what they ought to be. It would be in the interest of the contract itself that the Minister of Public Works should do as his predecessor did in the case of the customs house building, and provide for an eight-hour day. The work will go on more rapidly; which will be a benefit to Parliament and to the country at large.

I have very little objection to what my hon. friend has said with respeet to the fair wage clause. I shall be glad to take this up with the Minister of Labour, as I intend to do, before we get started, and ask him to arrange a schedule of prices for the labour engaged in the reconstruction of the building. The eight hour day arrangement is something upon which I would not like to make a definite statement until I have had an opportunity to look into it with the officers of the department and study what the custom has been in the past in this particular locality.

We must have Tegard to conditions as they exist; and, having regard to these conditions, we will treat the matter in the best light and give it very favourable consideration.
Public Works-harbours and rivers, Quebec- Anse a Beaufils-to repair breakwater, $1,450.

I had not expected to speak on any of these votes, but on this item for Anse a Beaufils breakwater I have something to suggest to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. I regret that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr.< Hazen) is not in his place, for what I have to say relates more 'to his department, but as the Minister of Public Works is the " master of . the Administration " he can give his orders to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. This Anse a Beaufils is a little cove on the Baie de Chaleur, in the county of Gaspe. I initiated the work there myself and happen to know exactly the conditions. This is an excellent little harbour for the fishermen. The fishermen on that coast go pretty far out in the gulf of St. Lawrence to fish, and as my hon. friend is aware there are more wrecks in that district, perhaps, than in any other part of the gulf of St. Lawrence. There is a bank there called the Orphans' hank, because of the many wrecks that havie taken place. This little harbour was built in order to give protection in time of storm, a harbour of refuge for the fishermen. I have visited the harbour on several occasions, and the fishermen have expressed great gratification that this harbour had been provided. But consider what has happened during the last three or four years. I received a letter a few days ago, and I saw the fishermen myself when I passed there last Thanksgiving day. The harbour is so good and is so well equipped that the fishermen from all the neighbouring localities, from Bonaventure island, from the county of Bonaventure, and even from neighbouring places in New Brunswick, when there is a storm in the gulf, make direct for Anse a Beaufils, and thus the fishermen of Anse a Beaufiils themselves are deprived of their harbour for the benefit of outsiders. Of course, a true fisherman must always 'be liberal and generous to neighbouring fishermen. Therefore, one of two things should be done by the department in this case, either to enlarge the harbour or give instructions to the harbour master	to limit	the	use of	the
place to the people of the locality.
I suggest to the minister that he widen the approaches of the harbour rather than limit the number of fishermen who may take shelter there. I shall be very glad if my hon. friend will note my remarks and instruct his engineer during the coming season to visit the locality and see what can be done in order to meet the exigencies of the case. I can assure him that this is a grievance on the part of the fishermen of the locality, because, although it is their own home, they are dislodged from it by their neighbours-good neighbours, as they are-from Gloucester and Bonaventure.

May I be permitted to say that I concur in the suggestions made by the hon. member for Rouville? These natural harbours will have to be enlarged or given additional protection if they are to render the service that they should. Our fishermen are numerous in Gloucester. We have two hundred sailing vessels going to the banks, and when the wind strikes in one direction they have to get shelter wherever the elements take them. I remember that complaint was made a few years ago by members from Prince Edward Island with regard to the harbour of Tignish, which was sometimes filled by the Gloucester sailing vessels. The Minister of Public Works at that time did enlarge the breakwater there, and now all the fishermen of Gloucester and Gaspe can get what protection they need in that harbour without causing any detriment to the fishermen of the locality. I hope that the minister will take this matter into consideration during the coming summer and see what can be done.	*

I have listened with interest to what the hon. member for Gloucester has said, as well as the hon. member for Rouville, in respect to this important harbour. I find that it is a rather important harbour of its kind; it is a harbour of refuge, and the population immediately affected amounts to something like 4,000. A considerable amount of money has been spent there, nearly $30,000. The amount asked for in the Estimates is simply $1,450 for the repair of the breakwater. Some work was done on the breakwater last year; $3,000 was spent. We have improved the breakwater, therefore, sufficiently, but we have not yet given consideration to the idea of widening the harbour, as has been suggested by my hon. friend. I shall be

glad to have the engineer look into it and see if there is necessity for it.

Parry Sound-in full and final settlement of Robinson, Walton and White's claim in connection with their wharf contract, $1,500.
What was the trouble there?

would be done by the Department of Public Works. I am sorry to say nothing has been done yet, except making surveys, soundings, and so on. Campbellton is rapidly becoming the most important town in northern New Brunswick. As the minister knows, it is the centre of the Intercolonial railway in that district, and has large lumbering operations. Its. population is increasing year by year, and the town is perhaps the most enterprising one in the whole of northern New Brunswick. Communication with the Quebec side is very difficult, being by flat-bottomed scows which can travel only at certain hours, owing to the low tide on the Restigouche river. When the Government took over the International bridge, which runs into Campbellton, we had hopes .that it would also take over the Gaspe and Baie des Chaleurs railway, and that the two would be linked up by a joint railway .and highway bridge. A couple of years ago or more the importance of this work was recognized. Hollowing the recommendations, an expensive survey was made in connection with the proposed undertaking, but the estimated cost of the bridge was so heavy that we did not feel warranted in constructing it two years ago, and that is still our attitude to-day. The work, however, is very necessary, and should be carried out when conditions change; but .at the present .time I do not think there is any hope either of the Public Works Department or of the two provinces concerned going on with it.

In addition to the point the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has mentioned with regard to the Grand Trunk, a similar arrangement might be made with the Canadian Northern with regard to their bridge at Isle Bizard. The same question has come up in connection with the Railway Bill that was brought down two years ago, and that ought to be made law now. The Railway Commission should be given power to order any railway to .allow a municipality or province to be joint builders with them of any new bridge; and I think it ought to go even further and provide that the public, whether acting through a province or a municipality, should be able to go to the Railway Commission andl have an order made that an existing bridge owned by a railway company, if it will bear the added strain, should be usable for highway purposes. (Translation.) Mr Chairman as the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway bridges between St. Anne and Vaudreuil, just mentioned, connect with the county of Jacques Cartier,

There is none other than at this point, and to-day any one going across from Montreal to Upper Canada must cross there, that is at St. Anne in an old ferry pulled by oars, to Perrot island and then take another ferry to cross from the island to Vaudreuil. I say without hesitation that such a methtod of travelling or transportation at this stage of our development is unworthy of Canada's progress. Any one going to the United States from Lachine or Montreal has to cross the river by way of the Victoria bridge and cover a long distance to no purpose whatever; while if the crossing could be effected from La-chine to Caughnawaga we should have the shortest possible route to the American side.
Last Sunday, intending to go to Chateau-guay-I must explain that between La-chine and the south shore the river is a little over a mile across-I was forced to go to Montreal, take the Victoria bridge, circle the lake in front of Laprairie, and come back opposite Lachine. I may he allowed to say that when I reached the Canadian Pacific railway bridge, on the road to the reserve at Caughnawaga, my car ran into a gully, and I had to get a team of horses to pull me out. duct. Starting from Montreal and taking by the driveways, one would get directly to Lachine, right opposite Caughnawaga. bridge is free. On the east we have the Victoria bridge, where we have to pay toll;

I urge on the hon. minister and on alii the members of this House who are interested in this question, to join together in common endeavour to realize those great public works which are necessary to the country's development, because obviously they would contribute to a large extent not only to the advancement of the counties which those bridges would tap, but also to the progress of Montreal, of the province of Quebec, and of the country a3 a whole.

I am very much pleased that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has brought this matter to the attention of the committee, and it gives me pleasure to back up a few of the statements that he has made. While this matter may not be looked on very seriously by many members of this House, I can assure gentlemen that it is of the most vital importance not only to the people of my county, but to the whole district, as well as to the city of Montreal. We all admit to-day that Montreal is the metropolis of Canada, and when we stop to consider that there is but one means of access to the city of Montreal by teams it certainly makes us feel that we are a little behind the times. Then there is another phase of the matter, apart from the international view that my hon. friend has taken, that is worthy of the consideration of this Parliament. I speak of the local phase of the question. My county, the county of Chateauguay, is very much interested in this measure. We have to-day throughout the greater part of Chateauguay and Huntingdon macadamized roads. In, my election in 1913 the question was put to me: "Will you assist us in getting direct communication with Montreal?" I said: " Friends, I will do my duty in that respect." I have attempted to do so, I have succeeded in obtaining certain works that were necessary along that line. But this question that my hon. friend has brought is one of great importance, and I am pleased to-day to endorse what he has said, and to attempt in. a feeble way to lay before this House the requirements of the southern portion of the province of Quebec. Situated as we are, as my hon. friend has said, we have to go almost around the city of Montreal in order to reach that city. We have to-day macadamized roads. a line of communication by auto trucks from my county and the county of Huntingdon direct to Montreal, but we were held up for want of direct communication. We come before this Parliament to-day asking to have this matter taken into consideration, inasmuch as it will benefit not only the southern part of the province of Quebec, but the city of Montreal as well. My county is one of the best in the whole province of Quebec for market gardening, and in that respect it could supply one of the greatest needs of the city of Montreal to-day. Hon. members are aware that the 'bulk of the garden stuff used in Montreal is imported from the United States. Why is that? Simply because the people in the immediate vicinity of Montreal have not free access to that city. If we had proper means of access to Montreal, the bulk of the farmers of my county would -be engaged in market gardening. They have the soil for it; they have people w(ho understand the work, but they require direct communication. I confine my remarks to this bridge between Lachine and Caughnawaga, inasmuch as it interests me and the people I represent, as well as the people to the south of us. If we had that direct communication we would, before two months, establish a line of trucks that would carry the produce of our counties direct to the city of Montreal, the farmers in Huntingdon and Chateauguay could load their produce on trucks in the early morning and place it on the Montreal market in the forenoon. This is a matter worthy of the consideration of this House, and I hope that the minister and the Government will take into consideration the appointing of such a commission as my hon. friend has asked for. Let us endeavour to do something for the southern part of the province of Quebec. As you all know, probably no other part of the province or the whole Dominion has received so little attention as the county I represent. The county of Chateauguay, as I said on a former occasion, has never come begging to this Parliament. The people of that country are independent people, and probably the necessity for Dominion Government aid has not existed in the past. But to-day the question presents itself in a light that I hope hon. members will realize. I hope they will give due consideration to this question and that before the session ends steps will be taken to give to the people of southern Quebec 
the accommodation which they 4 p.m. so need. This will be in the interest not only of the counties I have mentioned but of the city of Montreal. I tsincerely truet that the Government will give serious consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend.

I have no hesitation in saying that if there is a work in the nature of the construction of bridges in any part of Canada that it is desirable to carry out, this particular work takes first place. It is true, as the hon. member for Bonaventure has stated, that we also have to cross the canal. This is a work which belongs to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, if we are to regard it as an inter-

provincial undertaking. I . have had the pleasure of receiving large deputations from both Quebec and Ontario, who apparently have a very deep interest in the construction of this bridge. I appreciate the importance of the work for the island of Montreal. It is remarkable that that island, with its very great population of 700,000 or 800,000 people, has been able to get along so long without this communication between it and the city of Toronto. Recognizing the force of-the representations made in this connection, I take pleasure in saying that if the matter should be taken up by the twro provinces of Quebec and Ontario, I shall be pleased to join with them, as representing the Department of Public Works; and if we can do nothing else under our present law, we can always find some way fQr making grants to the provinces to assist in such an undertaking. A few evenings ago I brought up the question of the operation of the telegraph lines in the county of Victoria, and, on reading the minister's statement in Hansard, I found that he had stated that he deprecated what I had said. If I understand the meaning of the word " deprecated," it is that he did not believe what I said. I stated on that occasion that the telegraph line was improperly used during a provincial election, that it was taken charge of by the managers of the campaign, and that it was used for a whole month for election purposes without a charge' of one cent being made for the use of the lines, 120 miles or 140 miles in extent, and of all the offices and branches. I stated that as a matter of fact, and I ask the minister to believe me unless he can find any evidence to the contrary. I stated on my reputation for veracity in this House that that was true. I further state that the manager of the line, and of the largest office, has since admitted upon his oath in a court of law every word I have said. That is a matter of record in the courts of the province of Nova Scotia, and if the minister deprecates what I say I want him to look up the records of the court of Mr. Justice Russell, who tried the election case and read the sworn evidence of Mr. David Dunlop, who was the superintendent of the line, and the operator, who admitted on his oath that he had taken charge of the line, that he had not collected fees, that he had not made any return to the department, and that he had never been asked to make a return. These are absolutely clear-cut facts sworn to, and upon that I say I state my reputation as a member of this House. I do not want any minister to stand up in this House and say that he deprecates the statements made by a member unless he has evidence to the contrary.

Before my hon. friend goes any further I would like to say that I have read the report of my remarks in Hansard, but I can assure him that	what I	said had not the
meaning which he takes out of it. I do not know whether [DOT]the word was used or not, or whether it was used in the sense in which he describes it; but whether it was used or not, I want to assure .my hon. friend that I accepted his, word without any question at all in my mind that he

was stating exactly the facts as he found themw I wish to say to my hon. friend here that I regret very much to learn that such a state of affairs should have existed, and to assure him that I am looking into it, and I will see that it shall not occur again. It is an unfortunate position of affairs that our telegraph, lines in various parts of Canada are not as secret to the users as they should be. To my knowledge that applies to the large lines in Canada as well as to the local Government lines. Every effort should be made by every member of this House, and certainly every effort will be made by myself, to correct .such a condition as my hon. friend complains of, and, the facts being what they are, justly complains of. I will be glad to take every means to correct the condition and rectify it so that my hon. friend will have no cause for complaint in the future.

I thought from the hon. gentleman's tone of voice that he had no belief in what I said. The acoustics of this place are wretched, and you cannot always be sure what is said across the floor, and I thought that the minister did not believe what I was saying, because the word " deprecate," as I understand it, means that you do not believe a statement that is made. If the hon. gentleman says that he deprecated the action of those who would use the telegraph lines as I have stated, that is a different proposition altogether.

That is right.
Vancouver Island telegraph and telephone lines-extensions, $9,000.

I wish to ask a question or two with regard to the preceding items if I may... I notice, that there is a vote of $500 for repairs and improvements to the office building at House River in connection with the Fort McMurray telegraph line. What accommodation is there at McMurray, House River, Pelican portage, and Calling River for the telegraph offices? Are they in rented buildings, or does the.Government own the buildings?

I am afraid I have not that information. I will give my hon. friend the information that I have with regard to this particular item. This is an item of $500 for repairs and improvements to the office building at House River. District Superintendent McDonald, under date of the 21st October, 1915, writes as follows:
It has been found expedient, instead of erecting a building, to purchase from Fred Taylor,

House River, the building in which our office has been located. This action meets with appro, val of all the people. The building is log, 1G x 28 feet one and a half stories high and the addition thereto is 10 x 16 covered with rub-beroid roofing. The price paid for the building is $500 and the expenditure of another $500 will be necessary to put it in good repair.

This is not a matter of importance, but I would like to be certain if the offices at Calling River and Pelican Portage are merely offices in buildings belonging to private citizens or are offices supplied by the Government as at House River. Apparently the Government is going to own the office building at House River, and I wished to know what the situation was in regard to the other two places and also at McMurray.
The deputy will take a note of that and give my hon. friend the information. I could not give it to him correctly.
At McMurray, as well as the other two places. For the office at lake Saskatoon I see there is a revote of $400. Does the Government own that office?
Yes.

That is just for repairs
and improvements?	-

To complete the office
building at lake Saskatoon.
What are the rough details of the vote of $11,000 for renewals, repairs and improvements to the Peace River line, and is it intended to make the expenditure this year?

Yes. The $11,000 is required for renewing poles from Edmonton to Athabaska, 98 miles, at $100 per mile; for a well and repairs to the building at Grouard and for a well and repairs to the building at Peace River Crossing, $500 each.
Does the Government own the building at Peace River Crossing?
Yes.

Might I revert to the desirability of the extension of the line now running from Athabaska Landing via Plam-ohdonville to Lac la Biche and also to Lac la Biche station, which I mentioned a few days ago? Has there been any further consideration given to the suggestion?
When the matter was brought up on the last occasion in the House it was referred to the telegraph department, and they are getting a report. We expect to have it in a day or two.

I hope the department
will consider the matter favourably with a view to establishing a connection this summer, because it would be a very great convenience to the public and it would really be to the benefit of the revenues of the line. The Lac la Biche station is, and will be, a town and has railway communication. There is an important hotel there; it will be connected with the boating and fishing on the lake and in every way it will be very desirable to have telegraphic communication. The railway company do not intend to put in a telegraph service as they propose operating with the telephone. If the department can look upon this matter favourably, and can carry out this extension with a reasonable amount of celerity, it will be a great convenience to the public there.
We sent the department a copy of the remarks made the other evening by the hon. gentleman, and asked for a report. As soon as it comes I will let my hon. friend have a copy.
I am under the impression that I mentioned it last year and received a somewhat similar and equally favourable reply from the minister but so far there has not been any result.

We will see if we cannot arrange it this year.
Levis graving dock-further amount required, $3,000.
Is this for the old dock?
Yes. This amount is required for purchasing the blocks that go under the ships.

How are you getting
along with the new dock?

Pretty well. It is hoped the work will be completed this fall, but we are not quite sure.
Prince Edward Island-Bay Fortune-breakwater extension, $5,000.

My hon. friend from
Kings, who was obliged to leave, asked me to get some information from the minister. First of all, is this amount of $5,000 for the breakwater extension at Bay Fortune to be expended during the coming year? The vote would indicate that it is not for Tepairs, but for new work. If it is for an extension, I am informed that $5,000 would not go very far. Is the amount required for repairs or for extending the length of the wharf?

This amount is required for the construction of an extension to the breakwater at Bay Fortune. The work is required for the improvement, by securing, of a shoa'l sandbar at the entrance of the harbour, so as to facilitate the import of coal, lime, lumber, etc., and export of surplus farm produce from a large and rich agricultural district. During 1914-15 about $2,000 was expended in repairing and raising, for an average of 3 feet, the outer 300 feet of the old work; also placing in fenders, ties, ballast, etc., and covering the outer block. Foreman, W. Aitkens; rate of pay, $2.50 per day. The engineer evidently thinks we shall be able to do the work satisfactorily for $5,000.
What is- to be the total length of the wharf?
It does not appear to be given here.
What will be the total cost?
It is estimated that before completion it will cost $12,000.

Another question the hon. member desires me to .ask is why it is not proposed to go on with the construction of a boat harbour at North Lake, an item for which has been in the Estimates for quite a number of years, and to expend $5,000 alt Bay Fortune, when the work at North Lake is more urgently required and will be much more useful than the work at Bay Fortune?

With regard to North Lake, we have had a great deal of difficulty in getting the people to sign, for the right of way and the land required for the work. The question of damages has been in dispute for some time, and has not been [DOT]settled yet.

The minister must be wrong if my information i-s correct, because it appears by a return, I am informed, that the matter was adjusted to the satisfaction of the Government last June when tenders were called for.

The deputy informs me that my statement is correct. When we called for tenders we depended upon getting a bond from some parties indemnifying us against damages and so on, but we have not received it yet.

The hon. member for Kings is greatly impressed with the importance of repairing the breakwater at

Souris. He says that a year ago $144,000 was spent on an extension to the Souris breakwater. This, he says, is the most important public work in Prince Edward Island. A few weeks or a few months after the work was completed a storm of no more than ordinary violence made a breach in the -seaward side and carried away a portion of the new work, and every storm since has widened the breach. The hon. member is much surprised that nothing has been provided for repairs this year, and alleges that if the work is allowed to stand without being repaired, great damage will be done to the breakwater, and a great deal of money which has been expended will be lost. Has the minister any report with regard to the damage done to the breakwater, and is it proposed to ask for any amount this year to make the necessary repairs?

The engineer does not see the necessity for an expenditure this year, but later on something will have to be done. His report is as follows:
A contract for the 400 feet breakwater extension was awarded Beazley Brothers, Limited, on 18th October, 1912, at price of their tender, $143,917. The work was constructed according,, to plan and specification forwarded by the then District Engineer, J. B. Hegan. In November, 1914, when the work was nearing completion, 8 tiers of face timbers of the outer block became displaced from some cause which District Engineer Hyndman stated was difficult to explain, but was probably due to settlement. Mr. Hyndman certified that the work had been done faithfully and according to plan and specification, and that the damage was due to unusual and unforeseen circumstances. In July, 1915, the breakwater was again damaged by a heavy storm after the original breach had been repaired and reinforced according to specification. Consulting Engineer Hegan was then instructed to make an examination of the work. He reported that he did not consider that the injury sustained by the work resulted from either the use of poor materials or indifferent workmanship, but simply from unavoidable causes, as, so far as he could ascertain, the requirements and conditions called for by the contract, specification and plan, were fully and faithfully carried out.
Public Works-chargeable to income-public buildings, Nova Scotia-Halifax custom house, $2,470.

Would the Minister of Public Works please state what progress is being made with the proposed extension to the custom house at North Sydney? Last year, I think, there was a vote to build an examining house in connection with the custom house there. I did not notice whether the work went on or not. I know that they 'have a place rented in connection

with the building, but if the money is available a new building would be better.

Nothing is being done at present in this matter, and we think that for the present we can get on as we are.
Public buildings-rents, repairs, furniture, heating, etc.. $130,000.
Why this supplementary vote? Surely the minister knows what rents he has to pay. Why not include all in the main Estimates?

Since the outbreak of the war the staff has been very greatly increased, and the aggregate charge for rents is higher. But I may say, for the information of my hon. friend, in the first place, that we do not rent anything that is not absolutely necessary, and, in the second place, that when we rent we have a basis upon which the rental is fixed-we allow only enough to pay six per cent net return to the owner.
That would depend on who made up the estimate of cost.

The Deputy Minister of Public Works himself makes that up-gives special attention to it. This heavy expense for rents cannot be avoided at the present tipie-
Public Works-chargeable to collection of revenue-telegraph and telephone lines, Saskatchewan and Alherta-further amount required, $17,500.
What is this for?

This is to supplement an appropriation granted by Parliament last session to -complete payments in connection with the working expenses of the telegraph lines in. the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

This is for the last fiscal year. Is the minister allowed so long a time to make up the accounts for the year? As I recollect it, the Auditor General allowed a certain time, but it is nearly two months since the close of the fiscal year.
There is no fixed time, but the direction is given by the Auditor General. We are allowed until the close of the session, I understand.

And the time is not so long as I had figured-it is only a little over one month.
Miscellaneous-Royal Mint-further amount required, $43,000.

What is the purpose of this?
iSir THOMAS WHITE: The Mint has been doing a great deal of work during the past year for the British Government in treating gold that has been received from Africa and other parts of the world-I am not permitted to go into details for reasons that will be obvious. This $43,000 is the estimated additional expense. The charges made will, in a large measure, if not fully, reimburse the amount expended.
National Battlefields Commission-to supplement amount now available for purchase of lands, the acquisition of which has been authorized by Parliament, a sum not exceeding $10,-
000.
This is the matter to which reference has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the matter to which my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition drew attention the other day. It was in the original plan of the commission. The purpose of the appropriation is to. acquire certain properties there-Wolfsfield and certain other historic land's.
Hear, hear.

Has anything ever been done in connection with the lands left at the old ruins- at Louisburg? An English gentleman who died there -some years ago, Captain Kennedy, formerly of the British army, left some lands to be used for the purpose of commemorating the wars of Louisburg days-. In his will he made certain provision that the lands were to be utilized by the Dominion Government, subject to certain conditions. I do not remember just what -the conditions were, but they had regard to some action on the part of the -Government of Canada to put these lands in shape and to do some work around the forts that would put them in better condition. I have not the full details of the provisions of the will, but I thought that possibly the minister might bear it in mind in connection with the operations of the National Battlefields Commission.
-Sir THOMAS WHITE: The matter has not been specially drawn to my attention, but the desirability of some commission being charged with the duty of preserving historic spots is a subject which has been frequently discussed- in the House. I shall bear in mind what my hon. friend has said with regard to the Louisburg -situation.

I need not remind the minister that the -Society of 'Colonial Wars, which is an American society, has built a monument on those grounds. It is some part of what is being done to commemorate the old days at Louisburg.
Canadian Associated Press, $8,000.
Who is the European representative of the Canadian Association?
There has been no change; it is the same.
Are you aware that this does not include a representative in the old land?

John Ross- Robertson's
brother used to be the representative years ago, but I do not know who has taken his place since his death.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have taken this matter up with Mr. John Ross Robertson, as President, I think, of the Canadian Associated Press. My hon. friend will recall that, under legislation which expired some two years a-go, an annual grant was made to the Association from $12,000 downward; I think the last payment was in the neighbourhood of $6,000 or $7,000. Last year, instead of re-introducing the legislation-because I desired to discuss the matter with representatives of the press-I introduced an Estimate providing to -continue the amount which had been paid in the preceding year. This year the matter was again drawn- to my attention, and I have inserted an Estimate of $8,000, which is now before the Committee. I think that the object is one which appeals to us, especially at this time, because it is closely connected witlh the question of the news service from the old country. If ever there was a time when the newspapers ought to be helped by a justifiable subsidy, it is now.

We agree pretty well on the necessity of this vote. There was a time when newspapers in Canada were not satisfied with the service. A great deal of our news for some length of time used to come via New York, and we discovered that that was not the most reliable kind of information to get, particularly for Canadian consumption. I am a little out of touch with it; the member for South York would know the conditions as they exist now better than I would. I know that they were unsatisfactory for a time, but from a casual observation I should think that the service is more satisfactory now than it was some years ago.

It is very much
improved.
To provide for the administration of the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916: appointments for the purpose may be made without reference to the provisions of the Civil Service Act, $150,000.

This is an
important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This item is to provide for the expenditure in connection with the administration of the Business Profits War Tax Act which has been passed at this session of Parliament. When the matter was under discussion in the House, I explained in a general way the plan of administration which we had in view. The Act will be administered through the Finance Department. We shall have to add to the existing staff and we shall have to supplement that staff by officials in the several provinces. All business firms and corporations in Canada which have a capital of $50,000 and upwards will be liable to assessment, provided their earnings exceed 10 per cent in the case of private firms and individuals and 7 per cent in the case of corporations. The first thing to be done is to make a list from the publications of commercial agencies showing the firms which are likely to be liable to assessment. This has been done already by my department. The next step -will be to notify all these firms thought to be liable to assessment requesting them to make the return called for by the Act. In order to get the administration to that stage it will be necessary that \ the staff of the Finance Department be considerably enlarged and that additional officials be taken on in the several provinces. After the returns come in, they will have to be scrutinised and further investigation made in many cases in order that the final assessment by the department may be made. After the final assessment is made, notices will be sent out to the various firms and companies liable to assessment informing them of the amount of their assessment. Then there will be a right of appeal in the case of any feeling themselves aggrieved to the court of revision or board of referees referred to in the Act. It is not possible at the present time to make an accurate estimate as to how much the expenditure will be in connection with the administration of the Act, but it would seem to us that $150,000 would likely more than cover it. I cannot vouch for that statement, because I do not know the facts.	*

It is easily to be understood that the matter is rather tentative, and that at the present time my hon. friend cannot be expected to have an absolutely exa'ct plan to which he cares to give his authority. The minister must have a large clerical staff to perform the work arising from this new system of taxation. I think we should take some exception to the provision inserted, " appointments for the purpose may be made without reference to the provisions of the Civil Service Act." I do not think my hon. friend should take so much power as that. I am prepared to believe that some of these appointments must be technical, and that for them a technical business knowledge will be indispensable. As to these there may be special recommendations by my hon. friend under the Civil Service Act. But my hon. friend must have a large clerical staff attached to his office, and there is no reason why the provisions of the Act should not be applied. I am afraid that, under the administration of my hon. friends on the other side, the Civil Service Act is becoming largely obsolete, and that it is more honoured in the breach than in the observance. Still it is a very good law and one which I think ought to be welcomed by every Government. It saves every minister a lot of trouble, and it is a better way of insuring effective service than any other. Why my hon. friend should say that all appointments, even that of the merest clerk, should be made without conforming to the Civil Service Act, to me is incomprehensible. It is a very dangerous principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are some
considerations in connection with this matter which have been overlooked by my right hon. friend. In the first place, the administration of this Act is for a limited period; the Act is operative only until December 31, 1917. Therefore, we shall not be making permanent appointments, but only appointments of officials for the purpose of carrying out the Act during the limited period in which it will be in operation. I gave this matter a good deal of consideration, particularly this clause to which my hon. friend has referred. The difficulty which I encountered is this. We have to appoint officials in	the	several provincesto assist in the administration of this Act.	The	type	of official
that we should like would be men with experience in finance, such as accountants who are familiar with joint stock companies, or have had banking experience.
Under the Civil Service Act a man could not be appointed if he was over 35 years of age. It is going to be exceedingly difficult to get the right class of men to carry out this Act, especially at this 5 p.m. time, when the country is sending so many men to the front.
I am faced with a very real difficulty at the present time. Therefore I do not think my right hon. friend would suggest, in view of what I have said, that we should be confined by the regulations of the Civil Service Act in appointing the officials we shall require in the several provinces to assist us in carrying out the terms of this Act. Now I come to our own office. We shall require some accountants in connection with our office, and from the difficulties I have already experienced I am not at all sure that we should be able to obtain them under the Civil Service Act. In fact, I am sure we should not be able to obtain them. So far as clerks and typewriters are concerned, the employment will be temporary. Only recently I said to my deputy that we should retain the staff which, was temporarily employed in-connection with the war loan, to assist us in connection with the administration of this Act. There may be further war loans later on. The situation in the Finance Department at present is that we have a considerable temporary staff, which has been engaged in connection with the war loan, the last instalment of which was only recently paid. We shall endeavour to use that staff to the extent possible in connection with the administration of this Act; but we must have accountants and those having business experience if we are to carry this out at all successfully. My right hon. friend and I do not disagree so far as principle is concerned. But in connection with this measure, it is not my view that it would be practicable to obtain the assistance that we shall require under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, and consequently this proviso has been inserted.

I realize that a good many of the appointments must be technical-people who have special technical knowledge of business; but I am quite positive that under the Act as it exists today, section 21, if I remember aright, my hon. friend has the right himself to appoint, without referring to the Civil Service Commission, men technically qualified. But he has the Act to guide him, and he should use it. The temporary appointments are also covered by the Act, and there is no reason why the ordinary clerks, whether

temporary or permanent, should not be appointed under the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
Mr. MARCIL; Will these assessments on the companies be made payable at a certain period in one lump sum?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They will be
payable on November 1st in respect of the first financial period of the company or firm which is being assessed. Only one payment in one year is the principle.
The minister has not considered the idea of splitting these payments so as not to make them fall too heavily on those paying them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is aware that the Act does not apply except in the case of individuals, firms, or companies having at least $50,000 capital, and I think no hardship is likely to arise under the mode of payment provided for in the Act.
If there is only one payment in one year it will last over until 1918?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
In case the Department suspect that a statement submitted by any company is not accurate, what do they do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is why we have the official or officials in each province. We shall ask them to make an investigation and see the individual or firm or company in question and check up the statement to see if it is accurate.
After you get the statement from the corporation, you send out a statement of what you think the tax should be. Then if there is a dispute the Board of Reference comes in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would not necessarily accept the statement. If we had reason to believe that the statement was not accurate, it would be the duty of our officials to interview the party in question and check up the statement so made.
Before referring it to the Board of Referees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then, in'the light of the -statement and the checking up, an estimate would be made and notice sent to that firm: "You are assessed for so much in respect of the Business Profits War Taxation Act, 1916."

The department does all of this through its own machinery. In municipal assessments an appeal may be taken by one individual against the assessment of some other individual. William Smith thinks it is not equitable, and he appeals against the assessment of John Brown, say. Will that -sort of thing come into play or will the department take all the responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department will take all the responsibility. I do not think it desirable that that element' should be introduced. In municipalities one man can appeal against the assessment of another; hut, so far as Dominion taxation is concerned, that principle has not been applied. In matters affecting customs taxation, only parties in- interest are allowed to raise any question; otherwise you might have a situation which would lead to a great deal of petty controversy.
I do not think it would be a good situation. There is nothing to hinder a man from giving information to to the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Government and the party assessed are the only parties in interest.
Will the amount paid by each party be published or become known?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If Parliament desired returns as to the results of this measure, the returns would be brought down.
To defray the expenses of printing for dis. tribution 4,000 copies of the report of the Federal Plan Commission of Ottawa and Hull, $2,000.

I would like
to know, now that we have the plan of the commission, what are the plans of the Government in regard to carrying out what is suggested by the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend was not in the House the other day when the question was raised by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). I stated that I intended, as soon as the session was over, to take up the report of the commission, go over the ground, and give the matter my personal attention. I know that my right hon. friend is very much interested in this question. I fbelieve that a committee has- been appointed by the City Council for the purpose of taking it up with the Government at a convenient time. I am greatly pleased that the plans

appear to have met with the approval of the citizens of Ottawa and of the members of this House, so far as I can learn. It is generally considered that the commission has done its work well. My right hon. friend naturally asks what is the next step. So far as I am concerned, the next step will be to make myself thoroughly conversant with the recommendations of the commission, and the Government will be prepared to take up the matter with the city of Ottawa and to consider what step ought to be taken next. My right hon. friend is aware that the object of preparing this plan was that there should be a model to which the Government and the city 'of Ottawa, the city of Hull, and the transportation companies could work over a long course of years. It was thought that it would be of use to all the different bodies I have mentioned, and that is its chief value. But there are certain explicit recommendations which we shall have to take up with the view of seeing whether and when they should be carried out, and that is a matter to which we shall give consideration as soon as we can find time after the session is over. I have not had time during the present :ses-sion, since the report was presented, more than cursorily to glance over it, much less to go over it in detail.

I have looked over the Teport-I take some interest in this matter-and I must say that on the whole the commission has done very good work. There are some suggestions to which I will take exception-we cannot-all agree -but I am satisfied to know that the minister will take up the report of the commission and study it as soon as possible. I know that he has been very busy during the session, and he cannot be expected to do more than, take it up, after the session is over, with the committee of the city council. The work is very extensive; it is a work for years; and if something can be done now, it would be very advisable to do it.
To defray the expenses of the Economic and Development Commission, $25,000.
Will some one explain what this is?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is a commission which has been at work during the past five or six months studying economic conditions in this country, more particularly in regard to what preparation may be necessary for us in respect of the period
immediately following the conclusion of the war.
The Prime Minister says "us"; to whom does he refer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am speaking of the country, of course; it is very often referred to in that way. I hope my hon. friend does not take exception to it?
I wondered whether it meant the Government or the people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Their interests are identical.
Not always.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: According to the appreciation of my hon. friend, perhaps not; according to our appreciation, they are always.

Who are the
members of that commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The commission is under the presidency of Senator Loug-heed.
A good man.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The other members are Mr. Farrell, from British Columbia; Dr. Rutherford, from Alberta; Mr. Hopkins, from Saskatchewan; Mr. William Smith, from Ontario, a member of this House; Mr. W. B. Ross, a gentleman engaged in the fruit industry in Nova Scotia, and Mr. Rolland, of Montreal. They have a considerable number of people associated with them who are carrying on a great deal of research work and investigation. They are in touch with, the staffs of certain universities who are doing a certain amount of research work. Mr. William Pearce, formerly associated with the Canadian Pacific railway, has made a careful study of railway development in connection with land settlement, and has prepared plans which, I understand, are of a very important character, and which have been spoken of very highly by those who have had an opportunity of examining them. I have been asked to do so on more than one occasion, but I have not found time to avail myself of the opportunity during the present session. I understand from Senator Lougheed, who asked me to examine the work which Mr. Pearce has done, that it is of an important character. It has been submitted to. the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, who thinks it is so important that he hopes it will be extended to the other provinces.

Railway Commissioners in connection with the discharge of their duties. There have been reports made to me, sometimes written and sometimes oral, as to the work which the commission has carried on. Unfortunately, it did not occur to me that this item would come up at this moment, otherwise ' I would have prepared myself with some notes which are in my possession as to the really important work which the commission has carried on. I appreciate, of course, the fact that the duties entrusted to it are of so complex a character that it would be impossible in five or six months to make a careful or, comprehensive survey of all that must be taken into account by the commission in the discharge of its duties. Are they taking up the

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

The names of the commissioners, speaking for myself, are
