Customs-salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $3,590,000.
How many men are included in this army, and what is the significance of the words " notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act"?

There are 29,033 officers at
the ports throughout the Dominion.
What increase has there been in the number of employees?

There has been no increase; I have been decreasing them. There is a large decrease this year as compared with last. When men have gone to the front or vacancies have occurred for other reasons we have not filled the positions unless it was absolutely necessary; 300 or 400 vacancies that have occurred since the war began have not been filled. The revenue has decreased since August, 1914, but now, at some of the ports like Montreal, business is increasing; in fact, business at that port is greater than it ever has been.
Mr. MARCH.: Are the appointments in Montreal made under the Civil Service Act?

Mr. RElID: A man has to pass a qualifying examination before he can be appointed. Under the Civil Service Act preventive officers are exempt from passing an examination.
What is the significance of the words, "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act? "

The men at the different
ports work overtime, and under the law we should not be allowed to pay them anything extra, unless we inserted these words. Under the Civil Service Act we can pay them their salaries only, nothing for overtime.
What is the proper time of these employees?

At Toronto, for instance, from nine in the morning until four o'clock in the afternoon. Then they could put in two or three hours' extra work a day as landing waiters, at thirty cents an hour. Nearly every port is working overtime. In the Auditor General's Report you will see several items like this:	salaries, $900; overtime, $250.

Are the appointments at
Montreal made on the recommendation of the Collector of Customs at Montreal?
Every one who is appointed has to be approved by the collector and pass an examination qualifying for the position.
The hon. member, I take it, has read the evidence given before the Public Accounts Committee.
They are not responsible to us.
The Public Accounts Committee is not responsible to the House?
The minister is responsible to us.

Yes, I am responsible. There is nothing secret about this matter. The explanation was given in the Public Accounts Committee. Let me say at the outset that, as I stated in the Public Accounts [DOT]Committee, we had to get many things for the use of the first contingent. The Minister of Militia secured many articles from the other side of the line. He 'had asked me to arrange to allow these goods to come in at the different ports throughout the Dominion. There was a question of them being allowed to leave the other side, and be exported through Canada to the front. I gave instructions'-
Would that apply to clothing?

It applied to anything that
was required for the troops going to the front to fight for the British Empire, no matter whether it was clothing, munitions, guns or anything else. That was the instruction that I gave-that everything that was required to be transported through Canada for our troops that were to fight for the British Empire was to come in. And of course they would come through with the knowledge of the Militia Department, and by their instructions. I gave instructions to the Commissioner of Customs to allow this wherever the Militia Department wanted it done-at any port in Canada. The Commissioner of Customs did send one of his officials to Morrisburg to give instructions to the Collector of Customs. He wrote a letter and handed it to his official who went to Morrisburg, to read to Mr. Drew. But we were not at that time keeping records of letters and so on in order that they might come out at some future time. No one knew whether there might be some question raised as to these articles being allowed to pass through Canada.
Was it not explained to the collector that there was only machine guns?

If the hon. gentleman will
have patience until after I get through I shall be glad to answer questions.
Then let the minister not raise the question about the right of Canada to allow these imports.

It was raised in the press
everywhere at that time, whether munitions and other articles, including machine guns, might be allowed to be brought from the United States.

Let us get that cleared
up. That point was as to the right of the United States to let the goods go out, but there was no question as to the right of Canada to let them come in. Those goods were for us and for the Allies.

There might be a question
of allowing them to go out. We did not keep record of them-did not intend to keep a record of these goods passing through in bond
Why?

Why? I do not think it is fair for the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) to try to drag out of me a statement of the articles which did come over which were brought here for the soldiers going to the front. The Government had reasons at that time to try to get everything that we could, in the way of machine guns, ammunition,-anything that we could not get in this country-to help the militia that we were sending overseas at that time.

And the minister just
opened the custom house door wide to let in anything and everything, and allowed contractors like J. W. Allison to make all kinds of money that should have gone into the treasury of Canada.

It is all right for the member for Assiniboia to make that statement; but, whoever gave the hon. gentleman that information, I want to say that that information is absolutely false and untrue, every word of it. And let me say this also -that when the hon. member is outside, I will tell him to his face, if he should make that statement, that it is absolutely false and untrue. Such stuff was not brought into Canada in that way.

Does the hon. minister
know what was brought in?
The hon. member knows well what was brought in.

Does the hon. minister
know?

I know what was brought in; nothing was brought in except what was shipped to the Minister of Militia's Department at Ottawa, or to Valcartier camp, all of which went out of this country in the usual way. Not one single dollar's worth of goods was brought into this country except whait was brought in in the legal way and shipped to the Militia Department.

My hon. friend the minister has no more idea of what was brought in than any one else has. The door was wide open. The customs officer at Morris-burg said before the Public Accounts Committee that he knew absolutely nothing about what came in; that he did not know how many dozens or how many hundreds of cases came in; that they came in there and were shipped away by the scow load, thirty or forty at a time. He did not know what it was, whether machine guns, ammunition, clothing or anything else. If the customs officer at the port of entry did not know what was coming in, how does my hon. friend the minister know? The customs officer said that no records were kept of what came in. In the face of those facts, sworn to by the customs officer, how can the minister say that he knows everything that came in?

The customs officer said he
did not know what the contents of the cases were, because he did not open and examine them. That is absolutely correct, but the goods were shipped here to Ottawa and to Valcartier and the Militia Department have a record of everything that came in at Morrisburg, and the Valcartier Camp has. the same. The Government, therefore, is in full possession of the facts in connection with everything brought in at Morris-burg. The collector of custom at Morrisburg is an old man, seventy or seventy-two years of age-a fine old man; I am not saying one word against him. Instructions' were given to him t)o allow machine guns or any similar article to go through so long as they were shipped to the Minister of Militia or his department or to Valcartier camp. The goods that did come over came over between the time of the breaking out of war and October the 14th or 24th, just when we were getting the first contingent ready, equipping the men with machine guns and sending

them over in anticipation of their going right to the front. Was it not right and fair that we should give them the very best possible equipment? Yet because I, as Minister of Customs, assisted in getting these goods in and in having them shipped through Canada, the member for Assini-boia tries to make a mountain out of a molehill. I want to tell him and the people of Canada that any one who says that any goods were brought in at Morrisburg other than in a legal way and without the full knowledge and consent of the Department of Customs or without their knowing the contents, makes a statement that is not in accordance with the facts. I hope that the hon. member for Assiniboia will not try to mislead the people by making another statement of that kind.

The minister says that
the instructions given to the customs officer at Morrisburg were that he should allow the goods to come in free without taking any record or notice of them provided they were addressed to the Minister of Militia or to the camp at Valcartier. The evidence given before the Public Accounts Committee did not state that. The evidence was that the instructions given Mr. Drew by letter written by the Commissioner of Customs and handed to him by an official and taken back again were that all goods addressed to a certain bunch around Morrisburg should be allowed to come in free. Nothing at all was said about shipping them to the Minister of Militia or to the camp at Valcartier. It was said that the object of these instructions was to let the Sifton machine gun battery come in. It was shown afterwards that that battery came in not by Morrisburg but at Cornwall. So I say that the door was opened wide for anything to come in. How does the Minister of Customs know what came in? How would he know?

My hon. friend says that if the customs officer there had done his duty he would have kept a record. Did my hon. friend instruct him to keep a record? His instructions, as he swore to them, were that he was to allow all these goods, shipped to certain people, to come in without taking any notice of them and without making any entries. The minister now says that he should have kept a record. Will my hon. friend bring down a copy of the instructions that were given to the customs officer? If he does not do so, the man who received the letter of instructions, read it and was asked to hand it back again, should be able to remember what those instructions were. I hope that my hon. friend will bring down a copy of the instructions that were sent to the customs officer at Morrisburg. The fact remains that the door was opened wide; anything and everything could have been brought in, and I believe no one knows just what was brought in.

The customs officer was asked that very question, whether or not he suspected that any goods other than militia goods were passing through the' customs at Morrisburg free, and he said he had no suspicion whatever.
He said he knew nothing about them; he paid no attention.

He said he had no
suspicion. I put that question to him myself.

He did not examine
them; did not know how many.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In connection with the consideration of this item, and the succeeding item, providing for a loan of $15,000,000 to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, I desire briefly to give the House certain information which was asked for by hon. members opposite when this matter was last under discussion. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) asked me whether the certificate of the chief engineer of the Government had been given as to the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert. I find upon looking up the National Transcontinental Railway Act, and the agreement for the construction of this division of the National Transcontinental Railway, that no certificate is provided for as conclusive evidence that the road has been completed-whether or not the road has been completed is a question of fact:	[DOT]
The standard of the road Is not to be Inferior to the main line of the Grand Trunk railway of Canada between Montreal and Toronto, so far as may be practicable in the case of a newly constructed line of railway, and the road is to be constructed according to plans and specifications to be approved by the Government.
In this connection I may refer to the report of Sir Collingwood Schreiber, the chief engineer of the western division of the National Transcontinental Railway, of April 1, 1915, that is to say, a little over a year ago, in which he made this statement:
The western division-Winnipeg to Prince Rupert-has been in successful operation throughout since September 6, 1914. A very comfortable express train service has traversed the road twice a week each way, provided with the most modern design of sleeping and dining cars, in addition to which a passenger and freight service has been given daily on the road between Winnipeg and Prince George sufficient to handle the traffic offering.

Then he goes on to set out the balance of the work remaining to be done. In a word, I may say that the standard of the Grand Trunk Pacific while undoubtedly high is. not sufficiently high to comply with the requirements, that is to say, the standard of the Grand Trunk railway between Montreal and Toronto. For example, there are many trestle bridges which should be replaced by steel bridges. There are a number of structures which should undoubtedly be erected, but which are not indispensably necessary for the operation of the line. Therefore, answering generally the question of my hon. friend, I might say that, while the line is open for traffic, it is not up to the standard, nor is it likely to be for many years to come. According to the report of Sir Collingwood Schreiber, to which I have alluded, and to the facts as they exist to-day, I should say that some $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 at least would be required to bring the road measurably up to the standard to which I have referred. But on account of the financial conditions, to which I alluded in my speech, with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern Railway, it has not been possible, and I think it will not be possible for some time to come, to bring the road up to the standard required by the Act.
In connection with the Canadian Northern Railway Company's loan, I have since yesterday obtained from the Canadian Northern Railway Company a statement showing the estimated gross earnings, operating expenses, and net earnings for the years ending the 30th June, 1915, 1916, 1917, 1918, 1919, and 1920. As to the year 1915 and the year 1916, they bear out the statement which I made to the House yesterday, namely, that the net earnings of the Canadian Northern Railway Company for the fiscal year 1915, which ended on June 30 last, amounted to $6,623,000, whereas the estimated net earnings for the year 1916 are placed at $9,770,000. For the year 1917, Mr. Hanna estimates that the net earnings will reach $11,500,000; for 1918, $13,700,000; for 1919, $15,120,000, and for 1920, $17,700,000. Of course, these are estimates; I do not give them as my estimates, but as the estimates of the general manager of the road, made, I have no doubt, in good faith, according to the best information which he has available. I shall therefore lay them upon the table, because it would not appear to me to be necessary to delay considera-

tion of the items by printing these estimates.
Then, my hon. friend from St. John referred to the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific railway, questioning, as I understood him, whether it was a benefit or a detriment to the Canadian Northern Railway system.
The bonds of that railway were guaranteed by the Canadian Northern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They were guaranteed by the Canadian Northern, but I desire to say to the committee that that was one of the most profitable, if not the most profitable line of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Its earnings for the year ending June 30, 1915, were 5311,000, and for the nine -months ending March, 1916, they amounted to 5390,000. A note attached to the statement by Mr. Hanna is to this effect:
This company has a very heavy local traffic tributary to its own line quite apart from its great value to the Canadian Northern System as a connecting link for through business from and to the United States of America and Western Canada.
This line has also proved of great advantage to the Canadian Northern in that when Port Arthur elevators were congested with grain an outlet was found at Duluth. In no case has the Canadian Northern railway ever shipped grain to Duluth when such shipments could be handled at Port Arthur.
The increase in gross and net earnings for this year, compared with the previous year, is to a large extent made up from the movement of grain to Duluth during the congested periods at Port Arthur and this movement to Duluth was requested by the Board of Commissioners.
I lay this also on, the Table.
My hon. friend from South Renfrew asked me with regard to the amounts due to contractors. I made inquiry of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and I have received a letter from the assistant to the vice-president as follows:
With respect to the amount due constractors for work done, 'materials delivered and drawback on construction, the total of this is provided for either by cash on hand in trust accounts or securities available. We expect to largely liquidate these accounts within the next sixty or ninety days.
I may explain further to the committee that there remains in the trust account, that is to say the account in which were deposited the proceeds of the 535,000,000 of securities which -were guaranteed by the Dominion upon the Canadian Northern Ontario division between Montreal and Port Arthur, a credit balance of 51,300,000, and there is also a credit balance to the amount of 54,300,000 in the account, in
which was deposited the proceeds of the 545,000,000 of securities guaranteed by the Dominion two years ago. iSo it would appear that so far as the amounts due to contractors appearing in the statement of temporary loans and current obligations is concerned, with the measure of aid which we propose to afford, there will be funds available for their payment. I think that is substantially all that I was requested to furnish in connection with the further consideration of these two items.
Mr. 'GRAHAM: I notice that a considerable quantity of grain went south. I am surprised at my hon. friend boasting about that in connection with the Duluth road.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was not boasting,

I would have thought that he would consider it not a good thing for Canada that the grain should go south instead of coming east. As my hon. friend will understand, it is not an easy thing to go through these accounts and sift them. I was busy in the House last night and this afternoon, -and I have not had the opportunity to digest them. I suppose it would not be out of place for me to say, regarding both of these roads, that I do not take the pessimistic view that some people take as to the outcome of the situation, so far as the railways of Canada aTe concerned. There is no doubt that the war has dislocated things, and the traffic of the railways fell off to such an extent at one time that the strongest transportation company in the world, to my mind, the Canadian Pacific railway, saw its stock tumble to a degree that was never anticipated. That did not mean that the istock of the Canadian Pacific railway had not an intrinsic value greater than was represented by the figures shown on the stock exchange; but it did mean that for the time being trade was so dislocated- that the earnings, possibly temporary, were such that investment in the stock would not prove a paying one. But that condition has rapidly .adjusted itself. True it is that the great crop in the West has helped materially, and the transportation of munitions and other things connected with the war has done a good deal to aid the companies in increasing their revenue during the past year or so. But the substantial foundation on which our transportation companies must build will be the immigration into Canada, with which must come an increase of agricultural production, the tillage of a much larger acreage, and with all that an

increased output by our industrial concerns. I am not discouraged a bit about the situation. If conditions had remained as they appeared a few years ago, if immigration had continued to pour in, to open up out western lands and increase the cultivated acreage, with all the coincident development to which I have referred, the railway companies would he pretty busy at the present time. I have no fear for the future concerning them at all. At the present time we are facing a peculiar financial situation. The companies appear to be in a worse position than some other forms of industry, because we know all about them, and because they are of more gigantic proportions than many other businesses. But, as a matter of fact, a great many of the industries of Canada were in a very precarious condition when the war broke out. Instead of it being an injury to them, the war has been a godsend to them financially; but it has not been so until recently to the transportation companies. Take the Grand Trunk Pacific. The arrangement with that company was peculiar and somewhat complex, the late Government constructing half of the main line approximately, from Moncton to Winnipeg, a distance of 1,800 miles, while the company undertook, under certain guarantees, to construct the line from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert, approximately the same distance, I think the line from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert is not quite as long as the line from Moncton to Winnipeg. In addition, the Grand Trunk Pacific had to construct the system of branch lines to which I referred the other day. They have done that to a considerable extent, but not to the extent which will be necessary in order to feed the main line and in order that goods may come in, to be .shipped over these branch lines to the communities developed and yet to be developed.
The idea of building that road up to a very high standard elicited differences of opinion. I trust I shall not be 'breaking any rule of the committee if I deal with that for just a moment. There are two principles of railway construction. One is to build the cheapest possible road, practically placing the rails on the ties with little or no ballast, and with grades and curves of various dimensions, just so the road can begin to operate, and then, as it makes a profit, as the revenue begins to come in, it is used to improve the condition of the road and put in what we call betterments. In its former construction, the

Canadian Northern adopted the latter principles, and its branch lines all over the West and im the East, I think, were built on the basis of comparatively easy construction. When the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental came to be constructed, they decided to adopt the other principle, that is, to build a road of a very high standard at once, so that when it was completed it would be able to afford the people of the country cheaper transportation than possibly could be afforded them by a road built on the lines of cheap construction. I need not argue that, it is evident. We cannot tell at the present time, it can only be told as the days go by, how much benefit that superior construction is to the people using that road. It is conceded now by every person that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental form the most perfect transcontinental railway in America. I think that nowhere in the world is there a stretch of road of such length and of such superior construction as the Transcontinental line.
It is necessary, in order to utilize such a line, and to get the benefit of the dear construction, that it shall have a lot of business to do. It can haul a bigger tonnage with the same engine. It can haul more than double the tonnage that can be hauled for an equal distance over any other road on this continent at the present time with all the improvements. It will necessitate the filling up of the West as rapidly as possible, with all the coincident development. It will require that the industries and agriculture of the East shall be developed to the fullest extent. It will brjng a return benefit to them in the way of cheaper freights. The Government have proven, during the past few months, that they can afford to haul grain at a cheaper rate than it has ever been hauled for before. The rate of six cents per bushel from Armstrong, which is a point that corresponds with Port Arthur, to Quebec is a cheaper rate than was ever given before by rail, and the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) says that on that haul to Quebec a profit was made. This amply proves that the construction of a road of this character, if it has the work to do, is, for the present at least, of more benefit to the people than a line of cheaper construction.
It must he remembered too, Mr. Chairman, that ocean traffic has been greatly disturbed, and on ocean traffic, both Pacific and Atlantic, this through line depended

to a certain extent for its tonnage. But on the Pacific, as well as on the Atlantic, that traffic has been decreased to such a degree that the Grand Trunk Pacific and Transcontinental have received no benefit at all. Immigration that was flowing in by hundreds of thousands has come to a standstill. Increased acreage that, as everybody expected, would be yielding forth in abundance is not doing so, because the men are not coming in.
Then, many of our men from the West who were active in the tilling of the soil have gone to the war. In these respects conditions have altered to nuch* a marked degree that you cannot judge at all what would have been the result if these conditions had not so changed. In the years to come- and not so many years either-I look for a vast increase in the number of people who will come to our western country; I look to a development of British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, after a space of time following the war, that will astonish us all, not excluding the people who live in those provinces. Some of our friends are at the war; some have been killed and others have been wounded; others are in the thick of the fight and we do not know when we shall hear from them; others of our families, are preparing to go. On account of all these things, this is a time- and I say it advisedly-when we on whose shoulders the responsibilities of government is placed have to stiffen our backs to the burden and not grow pessimistic. Canada is all right; Canada is going to be able to carry all these burdens as the years go by; andwe must not on account of present surroundings and any temporary discouragements we may have let the public think we have lost confidence in the ability of our country to do what we started out to do, and that was to develop one of the greatest countries in the world. We must not lose sight of the fact that we' are a young and virile people; that under normal conditions we bring to our land the best; that our development, both as a people and of our natural resources, must go on; that we have inherent qualities in ourselves and in our natural resources that will make Canada what we expect to make her, and what to-day we believe she is capable of being made, if we will only stick to the helm and be true to our convictions.
This situation with regard to the railways comes to us at a time when we seem to be carrying the last pound that we can bear; and whether we agree to aid the railways in this or in some other way, my own conviction is that we all require some of the courage and stamina our fathers had when they first came to this country to hew out homes for themselves. Those qualities must be asserted in the sons yho have followed; we must rentain true to what -we believe to be our duty, and, that counse being followed, sooner than we expect it perhaps, we shall find that Canada needs all these railways, and will be able to use them for her own advantage and for the benefit of the people at large. In the years to come, for the Grand Trunk Pacific, with its magnificent construction, I look for a great traffic beginning in the east on the Atlantic and going right across to the Pacific, and vice versa. The Canadian Pacific Railway has done a large trade in that way and has made a name for itself the world over. No matter what we may have done by the Canadian Pacific Railway in years gone by, no matter how we may have criticised certain aspects of it, the fact remains that the Canadian Pacific railway is one of the greatest advertisements that Canada hae to-day. Wherever it goes its business is done in a manner that brings no discredit either to the business concerns of Canada or to the financial transactions in which that company is engaged. We have often been criticised for passing certain legislation in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway; but this much has always been in the minds of members of Parliament, namely, that the Canadian Pacific railway was a road that was creditable to the Dominion of Canada; and, whatever latitude was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway in the way of financing, whether we agreed with it or not, the company did not bring discredit on any person connected with it.
I have said these few things about the Grand Trunk Pacific. I have my own view about the way the Government has managed this end of it. But I am not going into that; I think it foreign to this discussion. I have strong views about the management of the whole Grand Trunk Pacific system as concerns Canada itself. Without saying anything imprudent, I think there are men in Canada who understand the Tailway situation and our transportation necessities as they cannot possibly be understood by men who do not live in Canada. Conditions here are so different, our development is so much more rapid and our territory so vast, that the circle in which we move, from a transportation point of

view, is altogether different to anything that could exist in a smaller country, with a denser population, and perhaps a more 'ntense production per acre. Our railway system has to cover many thousands of miles; we have a scattered population; we have a country only the fringe of which has been developed; and we must accommodate our transportation facilities to those conditions. To my mind we cannot rightly invite men from other lands to bring their families and go out into our vacant lands unless we are prepared to do something for them, so that they can get the production from those lands to a market that will bring them a good return. After all, what counts is the amount of money that a man has left over every year after paying his expenses. If we do not afford these newcomers the transportation facilities that will enable them to get the best value for their product, we reduce the value of their daily labour, and offer them no encouragement. When we understand, as we do, that the progress of our entire country depends primarily-primarily, I say-upon the man who is behind the plough, and upon the product of our soil, we can more thoroughly appreciate the necessity of allowing that man to get all he can out of the soil and out of his daily product, in order that he may be happy and contented. A man so contented is the best immigration agent we could engage in any place. It is true that during the past few years the condition of the man who tills the soil, and of his family, has been greatly improved by such conveniences as the telephone, and the daily mail.
But these conveniences only come to a comparatively few on the prairies; they do not have all these advantages in the remote districts. But, for the interest of the country at large, it is the duty of this Parliament, acting through its Government to devote itself with the utmost vigour as soon as the war ceases, to bring to our country a class of immigrants that will develop the country ae rapidly as possible. Thac will be good for our transportation facilities, good for the Dominion of Canada, and good for the Empire at large. If that is done, I have no fear-no matter what the temporary difficulties may be-of the final result to the Dominion no fear of the country's destiny. I have full faith that the Dominion will make such progress in all lines that all our railway facilities will be needed within the next few years.
Now, let us consider the Canadian Nor-
them along the same lines. I have been criticised, and the Government of which I was a member has been criticised, about, this railway. Well, you know, so many people have good hindsight, but not everybody has perfect foresight. Nobody could foresee that this war was coming, and nobody could tell what the result would be. We were all caught in a financial maelstrom. I am not discouraged with (the Canadian Northern as one of our transportation companies'. I did take exception with Sir William Mackenzie to. some of the things he was doing-for instance, to the extension of his lines through the Rockies; for the time being. But it is a condition that confronts us. I said concerning the Grand Trunk Pacific, so I say concerning the Canadian Northern-hard straggling now, but in years to come, and not so many years either, we will need the Canadian Northern to carry our traffic to and fro in the Dominion of Canada. In my opinion, the Canadian Northern west of the Great Lakes occupies the best territory of any of the railway lines running through the West, and I have been over a good portion of them all. While the system has been constructed largely on the principle I first mentioned, that of cheap construction, to begin with, and improvements made as traffic increased, it has a collecting system of close upon five thousand miles in some of the best territory in our Prairie Provinces. I may not agree with some of the projects of the Canadian Northern; and I do think it is time we came to a finality about handing them out money-I express that view frankly-but as to the final result, I believe that the Canadian Northern, running as it does through the best territory in the West, whether its operation is to be by the Government or by a company, will be needed in the time to come and needed to the fullest extent.
What is to be the outcome? The Government told us-and I suppose I am in order in discussing this now because it is practically the same subject-that it is the intention to appoint a commission to investigate the railway situation. I am not so confident at the present time that very much good will come out of that. And, by the way, I am afraid the Prime Minister will soon have to give up giving names to his commissions, which are now becoming quite an army; it might he more convenient to have them numbered or labelled. I am rather inclined to think that the Govern-

ment could, by calling in .the heads of these different companies, come to a solution of this problem without a highly-paid commission, and so could devote to some othe'r purpose the $150,000 proposed to be expended on the commission. But the Government says the commission is to be appointed. Now, the outcome will depend largely, first, on the instruction given to that commission, and, second, on its personnel. If the instructions are to examine the whole situation, without any restriction whatever, with a view to making suggestions to the Government as to the advisability of a certain policy and refraining from other policies, possibly that may be all right. But the commission must be composed of men of vision. We see it stated in the press that one commissioner is to come from Europe, another from the United States, these two to select the third. I do not know whether that is correct or not. I am not sure that men so selected will have the outlook that we in Canada have upon our own country. As I have said before, the men from the old land, to my mind, cannot possibly have the vision with which we are seized concerning the future of the Dominion of Canada, with our millions of acres still untilled, our mines unexplored, our vast timber territory, our fisheries, and many other things of whidh he is not cognizant-in fact, his vision might be narrower than that necessary to take in the whole situation; he might be inclined to bring the matter down to the present dollars and cents without having the outlook which, I think, is requisite if we are to, maintain the progress of the Dominion. The representative from the United States would be more in line with our ideas of development, I imagine, because his country has gone through what we are now going through. But it will depend altogether on the man. I submit to the Government that it is not going to be an easy matter to make this selection and to get men who will completely fill the Bill. These two, I understand, are to select the third. I would not let them do that if I were in the Government.

That is a very new idea.
Mr. GRArfAM:	That is in the press.
The press is energetic these days; it is getting something new, notwithstanding the occasional dullness of Parliament. Anyway, I would not allow them to do that. I do not wish to be offensive, but railway men, like all other combinations of business
men, are a kind of masonic society among themselves; and while the man whom they would select would probably work in harmony with them, he might not suit the requirements which, to my mind, ought to ' be found in any man occupying that position. The reason I speak of this is some experience that I have had. At one time in my career I tried to choose a board of engineers to help me in connection with the Quebec bridge. I selected one; we selected another, and before we had selected the third the other two were disagreeing. For two years I lived in an attitude that was not peaceful, the trouble being not in connection with the construction or the plans of the bridge, but in keeping my board on terms of peace with one another. The Government will have difficulty in the selection of that board, and the stronger the men the more difficulty there will be in getting them to work harmoniously, unless the Government handle the selection themselves.
I want to go on record as being a man with the optimistic view, wishing to sound a note of warning in my own weak way against our allowing ourselves to be stampeded by the pessimism that is in the air. Canada is all right. She is going , on to the accomplishment of her purpose with a firm tread. True, she is hesitating at the present time, but	when	those whocome after us write the history of our country I know that there will be no reason to feel ashamed of what the people of Canada did during this time of stress and trial. In addition to the courage we are showing concerning the war, we need just as much courage in handling our own domestic affairs. I urge upon Parliament the necessity of keeping our heads uplifted, not allowing ourselves to be diverted from the purpose of developing this country, feeling assured that in the years to come every dollar we have expended will be found to have been not unwisely expended, and will bring a return to the people of Canada, thus helping to build up our country as we expect it will be built up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are considerations affecting the credit of the Grand Trunk Company which are, of course, of great concern to its directorate.
9 p.m. My hon. friend knows that the guarantee of a company constitutes a contingent liability, and has a direct bearing upon its credit. I pointed out yesterday that the Grand Trunk had already given guarantees and made loans in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific to an amount exceeding $120,000,000. The Grand Trunk has to do considerable financing in order to provide betterments, improvements and terminal facilities in connection with Its own existing system; and the Grand Trunk feels, in a word, that it is not able, without seriously impairing its credit, to give additional guarantees upon the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend is quite logical in asking why the Grand Trunk should not carry the Grand Trunk Pacific. The reason they state is that they are not able to carry the Grand Trunk Pacific any further. Mr. Smithers made that statement in his letter to the Prime Minister, which has been laid on the Table of the House and appears in this statements It is perfectly clear that the Grand Trunk cannot, under present market conditions, finance the Grand Trunk Pacific by raising additional money upon its guarantee; and it ds their view that to do so would seriously impair the credit of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and prevent it from financing the betterments, improvements and facilities it requires in con nection with its own system.

I wish to state, with
the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Graham), that I also am an optimist. I have faith in my country, and I am far from being inimical to any of the railway systems. I think they have done a great deal towards the opening up and the development of this country. I cannot forget, when I was a boy attending Ottawa University, spending my evenings in the House of Commons listening to Sir Charles Tupper, Sir John Macdonald, Sir Richard Cartwright, and the other giants of those days. It was at the time of the inception of the Canadian Pacific railway. I remember Sir Charles Tupper predicting that some day the crop in the Northwest would yield 100,000,000 bushels. There was a roar in the House and in the party press over the prediction of Sir Charles. They derided him as too great an optimist; but he lived long enough to see his prediction fulfilled. My hon.

friend will remember that the Canadian Pacific was in pretty low water on a certain day. I remember that when the Hon. Frank Smith was a member of the Macdonald Government, and when the late Lord Strathcona, then plain Donald Smith, was connected with the company, together with Lord Mountstephen, they approached the Government on a very notable occasion when they were nearly bankrupt. The Government had refused to make a small advance, that is, small compared with the advances that have been made to railway companies since. They asked for $25,000,000. The history of the cabinet meeting of that day has been told by many writers, but perhaps the House will bear with me if I recall that the advance-I think it was something like $25,000,000, but perhaps my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) will be able to give the exact figure; he knows that part of Canadian history better than I do-had been refused by the Government at Ottawa. It is said that Donald Smith, afterwards Lord Strathcona, and Lord Mountstephen returned to the Russell Hotel in very low spirits. In fact, they were ruined, and their company was facing bankruptcy. But the Hon. Frank Smith-and all honour to his memory-and the late Hon. Mr. Pope, father of Senator Pope, asked Sir John Macdonald to hold another cabinet meeting to reconsider the application. It is said that at that cabinet meeting it was declared that if no advance was made the Canadian Pacific railway would go bankrupt, and that if the Canadian Pacific railway went bankrupt the credit of the country would be seriously damaged. We all know the sequel. The advance was made; the money was refunded before the day named in the contract; the line was built, the last spike was driven in near Vancouver by Sir Donald Smith himself long before the date fixed in the contract, and 'to-day the Canadian Pacific railway is certainly the beet administered corporation on the/American continent, and possibly in the world. I am bound to say that the heads of the Canadian Pacific railway have always been men of the highest merit, and the officials also have been of the very best. Having read the history of my country since Confederation and having lived since the inception of the Canadian Pacific railway and watched the course of events up to the present time, I am an optimist and believe that our National Transcontinental can certainly be saved. But it is not pessimistic to state 
that nationalization is ripe. I believe in nationalization, in state ownership, as regards railways. The note of pessimism comes from the Minister of Finance. It is not by listening to speeches on this Slide of the House that I become pessimistic; it is by listening to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. He tells us in so many words, if I mistake not, that these proposed loans of $8,000,000 and $15,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern are a stop-gap; that they are only to enable them to pass through the crisis, and that we may well expect that in the near future they will come again hat in hand to obtain new loans from the Government of this country. So that I gather from the remarks of my hon. friend that he has in mind that, as surely as day follows night, the two systems are doomed, which I do not believe. But if they are doomed, why should we make the loans to-day? Why should we increase the burden? I will give some advice to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and to my genial friend the Acting Minister of Railways, and I will charge nothing for it. The Government knows to-day that these two systems are in deep water. They have come again and again to this Parliament to obtain advances. The Government practically promised on each occasion that it would ibe the very last time and that their claims would not be entertained again. They come again this year, and, with this note of pessimism in the speech of the Minister of Finance, let me assure him that four out of five men on the street will tell him that the time has come for this country to get hold of these railway systems, to nationalize them. If my hon. friend will put his ear to the ground he will find out what he has to do. He will appoint this commission, he will delay the loan which he intends to make, and he will begin by putting that commission into operation. Let us prorogue this session of Parliament, let us have a session inside of four or five months, and then, if the report contains what seems to be already in the mind of the Minister of Finance, let us go in for nationalization. Otherwise, you are simply adding to the burdens of the people, you are not practically helping the two railway systems, as you will have in the end to nationalize them. I have it from the highest railway authority on the American continent-and if I were at liberty I would give the name, but I am not-that the Government must, within a very .short time,

take over the transcontinental railways and have three state-owned railways.

When the Canadian Northern guarantee (proposals were 'before Parliament in 1914, I took exception to the position in regard to the branch lines in the Prairie West. I would like to know what the position is, what is going to be done under this proposal now before the House in regard to these branch lines of the Canadian Northern in the Prairie West, branch lines not yet completed, although bonds guaranteed by provincial governments have been issued. In the Government's proposals of 1914 they simply ignored that condition. They counted the bonds which had been guaranteed by the provincial governments as an asset of the company upon which they took security, but they took no measures to secure the completion of the branch lines. What (has the Government in mind in the proposal now before the House in regard to these branch lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The present proposal has no bearing on that matter at all. The question of whether the Canadian Northern will be able to complete these branch lines will depend upon its ability to finance the securities guaranteed by the provincial Governments. It is quite possible, although I am speaking without full information, that if the financial conditions permit, the Canadian Northern will be able to proceed with the lines in question; but this loan is for the purpose of meeting the current obligations of the 'Canadian Northern and to enable them to finance until the next session of Parliament. The company is confronted with an immediate serious situation by reason of the large amount of its unfunded debt and current obligations, and this loan is for the purpose of meeting that situation and enabling them to finance during the year. Whether the Canadian Northern will proceed with the branch lines in the West under any understanding or agreement with the provincial Governments will depend entirely on its ability to finance the requirements altogether apart from this particular loan.
I do not think that the position taken in 1914, or the position taken just now by the Minister of Finance, is fair and reasonable or is even sound public policy.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does not my hon. friend observe that in order to provide for what he has in mind the Government would
have to give an increased amount, assuming that we agree that this money is needed to keep the railway system as a growing concern? If the Government would provide an additional sum specifically for the purpose in question, that is one thing; but the Canadian Northern railway, as I stated, finds itself in such a position that it has to have this -aid in connection with its current obligations and unfunded debt.

What the minister says does not apply exactly, because I know that in some of the provinces the railway company has sold these bonds guaranteed by the province and that the money has been deposited in the bank and can only be drawn out on the 'certificate of the provincial Government's railway engineer. There are some millions of dollars, raised by the railway company from the bonds guaranteed by the province, lying in the bank, and the railway company does not complete the lines for which these bonds were issued. That was the ease last year and it is the case to-day. If the Government is going to come forward like a good parent and practically finance this company, it ought to see that the -company spends the money lying at its credit in the bank to complete these railways, or complete them as far as the money will go. , There is no sense in the money lying there, and settlers on the prairies not being able to get the railway accommodation for which the provincial -bonds were sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will, I am sure, realize that it is a question, from the Canadian Northern standpoint, as to whether they can build the lines that were intended. I accept the statement of my hon, friend, although I have no accurate knowledge as to the facts, that guaranteed bonds have been sold and that the money lies in trust account to the credit of the Provincial Treasurer for the purpose of constructing these lines. Let us assume that the money is not sufficient for the purpose; the Canadian Northern have to have regard to the existing financial conditions and it will be for them to say whether the money is sufficient for them to complete the line. They might say:	"If we go ahead and
build the line we can only build it up to a certain point, and we will have to stop there owing to existing financial conditions. We are not able to raise the additional money to build this line, nor is it desirable that under existing conditions we. should incur the loss which

might result from the early operation of the line." The difficulty of this war time is that the railway companies, as well as other companies, are confronted with extraordinary financial conditions under which they are not able to do what they would gladly do if the conditions were different. If they were able to finance as they were some years ago, and if their prospects were such that they could carry on the operation of these extra lines, the situation would be entirely different. But under present conditions I can well understand any railway company, either the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern railway, unable as they are to market their bonds except at rates away below the price they could have got two or three years ago, proceeding with construction without the certainty that they would be able to finish the lines, or without the certainty that after the lines were finished the company would be able to bear the additional burdens until such times as the lines were remunerative.

Again, I say, I cannot
agree with the hon. minister that the two questions are entirely dissociate. I insist that they are absolutely interlocked; that the question of what the Canadian Northern railway is doing with the money of the provinces that it has in hand, and which this Government counts as an asset

speechtext: No, it does not.

Under the guarantee of
1914 that money is listed as a security held by this Government on the Canadian Northern railway. Having assumed that position, this Government have a responsibility in regard to those enterprises that they cannot ignore, and which they should not ignore when there is before them a general proposition of aid to the Canadian Northern railway. This proposition of aid to the Canadian Northern railway is not confined to interest payments. It includes not only interest payments, but payments of actual expenditure. If the proposition were confined entirely to interest payments, there might be some merit in the contention of the minister. But it is not confined to interest payments; it includes payments for work done, for accounts outstanding, and other liabilities. It goes beyond the question of meeting interest payments now accruing and takes into account these other considerations, and I maintain that the question of the completion of these branch lines is not only of equal but of vastly

greater importance to the well-being of the country and the success of the Canadian Northern enterprise, and the security of the money that is invested in that enterprise, than any of these other considerations. I hope I shall be excused if I speak very strongly on this point, but I do so because my constituency is very very deeply interested, as is also the adjoining constituency.
This railroad question has generally been discussed by those who see the question only from the centre outwards; I represent the people who are at the outside of the circle, and who are affected in an entirely different manner. Thousands of people have gone into the partially wooded country north of the Saskatchewan river, along surveyed routes of the Canadian Northern Railway, knowing that the bonds had been guaranteed by the provincial Government, knowing that the bonds had in many cases been sold and the money realized. They would not have gone in there and settled if they had not had the expectation that the road would be completed within a reasonable time. The company have in one case built and opened up some sixty miles of road, and graded some fifty miles more, but without the steel. In another case they have sold the bonds for a hundred miles of road, and have graded eighty-five miles, but have laid no rails at all; and people for a hundred miles beyond the extreme end of that grading have gone in and settled upon the expectation of the road being built. How the Government, holding 40 per cent of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway-have assumed that much responsibility in regard to the company-can absolutely ignore that condition and say: We have no responsibility whatever in regard to it. We know nothing about it; it is a matter between the Canadian Northern Railway and the provincial Governments-is something I cannot understand. At the time they are saying that, they are taking the money of those very people to pay the Canadian Northern liabilities, and not liabilities merely in respect of interest accruing, but capital liabilities incurred in other localities. I have no hostility to the Canadian Northern Railway, and in this matter I do not wish to criticise the Government severely, I appreciate the difficulties that have to be faced, and am willing to assist the Government in facing those difficulties, but I certainly cannot agree without protest to a proposal that would carrry aid a certain distance and

chop it off just where it touches the people whom I represent, and who are more deeply-interested in the extension of aid than any other people in the Dominion of Canada.
The idea that the Provincial Governments of the Prairie West are primarily responsible, or ought to be primarily responsible, for the railway development of that country is not a fair proposition. The land, the timber, .and the minerals of the Prairie West belong to the Dominion, and are administered by this Government. The provinces do not own a foot of land, a stick of timber, a pound of coal, or a cubic foot of gas; they have no right of proprietorship in any of these things. The Dominion at large owns all these resources, and this Government .administers them, derives revenue from them, and is responsible to the country for their development. In response to the demands of the people who were actually settled on the land, and who looked to the Provincial Government for means of transportation by wagon roads, it is true that the Provincial Government, considering the situation of these people and realizing that wagon roads could not possibly meet their requirements, guaranteed railway bonds, for the purpose of having railroads constructed. The Provincial Governments have done everything they could; they have strained their credit to the limit for the purpose of aiding in the construction of those roads.-a purpose which has had for its result the bringing into immense value of the property of the Dominion of Canada. This Government has guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern Railway, and, the railway company having sold the 'bonds and having spent a laTge part of the proceeds; but not the whole of it, this Government takes a blanket mortgage on the very roads that the Provincial Government has guaranteed; and this Govern ment, now calling on the people of the Dominion to contribute $15,000,000 for the aid of that railway company, absolutely ignores the condition I have placed before the House, and the position in which these people are situated. I cannot agree with the Minister of Finance that this is not < the concern of this Parliament or of this Government. I consider it an absolutely intimate concern of this Parliament and of this Government. Looked at only from the standpoint of the Canadian Northern Railway-if that was the only interest to be considered-the completion of these branch lines-I am not speaking, remember, of lines that have not been begun,
but of lines that have actually been commenced, and wihich stand "partially but not finally completed to-day, either for shortage of money or other reasons, I know not what-I maintain that the completion of these branch lines would be of greater material benefit to the railway company itself, in the way of building up the traffic that is necessary to its ultimate success', than any other assistance that could be given to it by this Government. I hope the Government will reconsider this view that has been expressed. When I saw this liberal amount of aid proposed for the Canadian Northern, I naturally concluded that it was intended to consider the position in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and that some adjustment would be included that would tend, at any rate, to the completion of these partially-completed enterprises.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Is the hon.
member speaking of the two companies, the Canadian Northern Western and the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan?

I am speaking' particularly of two lines in Alberta, in my own constituency and the adjoining constituency, which are under the Canadian Northern Western charter, I think; but I take it for granted that there is a similar situation in Saskatchewan, though I am not familiar with it; and I know there is a similar situation in other parts of Alberta, where the country is in occupation and is under production, and where that production is absolutely handicapped for lack of the completion of Canadian Northern lines which have been guaranteed by the provincial government,-the people have gone in and settled there in expectation of these lines being completed. I am not accusing the company of bad faith-but I am stating that there is the condition, and I say it rests upon the shoulders of this. Government to see to it that that difficulty is rectified under present circumstances.

I will certainly not
deny that there are districts in the West which are in need of branch line construction. Furthermore, it certainly would be our duty, were it in our power, to see to it that all branch line construction now necessary in the country is completed. The hon. gentleman thinks the Government is remiss in its duty in bringing down this measure without seeing to the completion of certain lines in the province of Alberta, and complains that the matter of their com-

pletion is entirely one for which this Government is responsible. He refers to a couple of lines which, he says, are under the charter of the Canadian Northern \vestern, in respect to which he says the bonds have been guaranteed to the extent, of $15,000 a mile by the province of Alberta, but which lines have not been completed.
. \
I have to protest against the conclusion of my hon. friend right there.
That Parliament came to the conclusion-
That it came to that conclusion at my insistence.
Not by my intention anyway.

Perhaps the hon. member's intention, though he argued in favour of that, was that we should decide against it. However, we agreed with him on that occasion, and, as a consequence, the Canadian Northern Western is still under the authority of the provincial Government of Alberta.

I hope the hon. member will permit me to interrupt him just a

moment in order to get the record Tight. I think Hansard will prove that I insisted, in the remarks I made, that if the Government took the steps they did at that time they should assume full responsibility for the railway.

But he insisted that the control of the Canadian Northern Western should rest with the province of Alberta. Perhaps he would have liked that we should assume responsibility for supplying the money; but he insisted, whether we supplied the money or not, that the Government of Alberta should have the authority.
I cannot agree with that statement of the case.

The hon. gentleman is endeavouring to give the House the impression, if I caught his argument correctly, that the proceeds of securities guaranteed by the province of Alberta had not only not been utilized for the purpose for which they were guaranteed, namely, the completion of the construction of lines covered by that guarantee in the province, but were diverted to the payment of other debts.
No, I said they were listed as part of the securities over which this Government assumed control in consideration of the guarantee given.

The Government mortgage of 1914 applied to all the properties of the Canadian Northern, or, moTe strictly, it did not apply on the properties, but on the stocks of the company, subject to the mortgages, and the mortgage was in favour of the Government of the province of Alberta as security for its guarantee. It would be impossible that there should be any diversion of the funds; the funds are expended on the roads, or they lie there awaiting expenditure. If they lie there, it will be for one reason, and one Teason only-that they were not sufficient to construct the road. The hon. gentleman has been instrumental in seeing to it that the province of Alberta kept within itself control of that road. The province of Alberta is not without power yet, if it insists upon the completion of these lines which the proceeds of the guaranteed securities are not sufficient to complete-it is not without power to increase that guarantee and so enable the proceeds to be made sufficient to secure completion. I understand that the policy of the road has been to build such lines as were laid out' at the time of the going through of the $45,000,000 mortgage of two years ago, but

not to prosecute further unless the proceeds of the securities already guaranteed were sufficient to enable them to complete; for the simple reason that it has been the practice before to realize on provincially-guaranteed securities to the fullest extent possible and then to use the proceeds of the consolidated debenture stock to complete construction.
It is not a question of the Canadian Northern going forward with lines not already begun in 1914; it is a question of the company completing lines then begun and partially completed.
In one sense, I presume, a branch line is never completed. It may extend for ten miles, and later for another ten miles, and so on.

To the extent to which
bonds have been issued.

To the extent to which there is money to complete. That is as far as they are able to go. The consolidated debenture stock mortgage provides that there may be a priority to it of securities to the extent of $10,000 per mile issued, or $15,000 per mile if those securities are guaranteed by a provincial or by the Dominion Government. The consolidated debenture stock securities become a second charge, subject, say, to provineially guaranteed securities to the extent of $15,000 per mile. Consequently they are able to issue that stock subject to these provincial securities. But the trouble has been that since the outbreak of war it has been impossible to sell that character of stock, so that there are no moneys that would enable them to ' go ahead with that construction. If the Dominion Government were to ask them to do so, the obvious answer would be: supply us with the funds, and we will. If the bon. member for Edmonton wants us to take the position that in addition to what is absolutely necessary to hold the situation we should provide the railway company with funds to prosecute new construction or to complete the prosecution of construction for which tthe provineially-guaran-teed securities are not sufficient, then he should put that in the form of a definite resolution so that we shall know what we are asked to do. For the present it is not the intention to provide funds loaned by the Dominion of Canada to prosecute construction further. The provincial Government has it in its power to do so. We have power under the legislation of 1914 to give priority to provincial securities to a
greater extent than they have already been issued, and I have no doubt that any application to give such priority to provincially-guaranteed securities would be sympathetically considered. The provincial Government has it in its power to enlarge that guarantee and to give priority to that enlarged guarantee if it so desires. So that it has the situation in its own power.

The minister has stated
my position exactly. Under the circumstances as they exist, the Government being a part owner in the Canadian Northern and assuming to carry the Canadian Northern forward, I think that that would be an entirely proper additional expenditure on the part of this Government. I desire it to be understood exactly in the terms that my hon. friend has stated; that is exactly the position as I view it. When the Provincial Government guarantees the bonds of a branch railroad to the amount of $20,000 a mile and the company sells those bonds, no doubt at a considerable discount, and spends a part of the .money-we do not know how much-the remainder of the money is to the credit of the company at the order of the provincial treasurer. My hon. friend says that if that money was sufficient to complete the road the company would complete it. It does not follow at all that the company would complete the road if that money was sufficient to complete it. It may be that the financial circumstances of the company are such that; the money being deposited in, we will say, the Bank of Commerce, the Bank of Commerce is willing to advance money to the company for other purposes while that money remains in the Bank of Commerce, a satisfactory collateral to the loan that is made for other purposes.
The hon. gentleman knows that it could not possibly be applied as collateral to any other loan. The trust deed would prevent it.

I do not follow my hon. friend's argument. I know that papers could not be drawn to that effect, but I know also that the management of the bank recognizes-$3,000,000 being there to the credit of the provincial treasurer of Alberta, whicih money cannot be drawn by the provincial treasurer until certain railroad construction has been done-that if they have an understanding with the railroad company that railroad construction will not be done, the money is just as safe in



the hank for other purposes as if they had all the agreements that could be put under seal.
That might be, but it could not be there as collateral to the new loan.

I am not a banker, and I may be using the word " collateral " improperly. I am sure, however, that it is perfectly good security to the bank to enable it to advance the company money for other purposes, and I verily believe that is what has been done, not so much because the bonds did not realize enough money to enable the company to build the road as because the necessities of the company caused that money to be used in the way that I say, for purposes other than those for which it was intended and for which the provincial guarantee was given. I have taken the responsibility of bringing this condition to the attention of the Government and I say that it is a condition that demands attention at this particular time. If the Government say: "We have no interest in this matter; we care nothing about how the Canadian Northern juggles with their money or with the money that they get from the provinces; if they are able to use provincial credit for the benefit of Dominion enterprise, well, that is good business; let the provincial Government find their own remedy;-if the Government say this, I do not think it is a fair proposition. I do not think it is right; I do not think it is good business. I certainly know that it is not good for the progress of the country, nor is it good for the Canadian Northern Railway Company itself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: One would think that if there was any such collusive agreement between the bank and the railway company within the knowledge of the provincial Government, they would simply remove the money so that it would stand to their credit in the same way in another bank.

That is quite an obvious conclusion, but there is this to be said: on a certain occasion not many years ago the provincial Government of Alberta undertook to do that very thing in Tegard to a railroad aid transaction that was not connected with the Canadian Northern in any way. The result was that the bank refused to give the money up. The case was carried to the Privy Council, and the Privy

Council decided that the Government could not draw the money from the bank. Having had that experience, they are not anxious to undertake it again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend entirely misunderstands me. I did not suggest that they should divert it to any other purpose. The Privy Council did decide that they could not divert it to any other purpose under the particular circumstances, but the Privy Council did not decide, nor did any other court decide, that the money could not be placed to the credit of the provincial government for the same purpose in another bank which had no collusive arrangement with the railway company.

I am not able to answer
the Prime Minister; he,being of the legal profession, I will have to bow to his interpretation of the Privy Council's decision. But he will pardon me if I say that I do not appreciate the condition as he has stated it. I cannot see how the question as to how the ultimate purpose for which th'o money was to be used came in, when thr only question was:	shall the Royal Bank
be compelled to honour the cheque of the Provincial Treasurer of the Government of Alberta, or not? I cannot understand how the purpose for which the money was to be used came into question. At any rate, that is what occurred, and because it occurred the provincial government is not anxious to enter into litigation with any of the banks on that account. This money got-into the banks before the decision of the Privy Council in the Great Waterways case was rendered, and I imagine that probably it will not occur again.

I am neither an optimist nor a pessimist so far as railways or anything else are concerned. I only want to see the Government doing the best that is possible under the circumstances of this difficult railway situation, and for that reason I want to get whatever information I can.
I noticed a statement in the Bureau of Railway News Statistics, Chicago, that the Government-owned railways in Canada in the last year cost $102.13 for each $100 taken in; and the private-operated cost $73.94. That is not an encouragement to me for Government-owned railways, nor will it be until we have some system of operating them to better advantage than we have had in the past.
The Canadian Northern statement does

not show in what proportion this $15,000,000 is to be divided between payment of interest npon securities of the companies included in the Canadian Northern Railway system having priority over the guaranteed securities authorized by chapter 20 of the statutes of 1914, instalment of equipment securities, and upon construction. I think it is quite material for us to know how much of this is to be used for these items; we cannot otherwise discuss' it intelligently.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will find on page 13 of the Canadian Northern statement a memorandum, prepared from records of the Finance Department which I had prepared, showing the disposition of the proceeds of the $45,000,000 of guaranteed securities. I think my hon. friend may assume conclusively that the proceeds on the $45,000,000 of guaranteed securities have been paid out in accordance with the legislation of 1914 and the trust mortgage executed in accordance with its provisions. As to the proposed disposition of the $15,000,000, I draw his attention to page 8, on which appears the most important statement in this document, because it shows the immediate financial situation of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. So far as the funded debt is concerned, of course the securities have been placed, but the urgency of the situation of the Canadian Northern Company's system, is shown by the statement on the lower part of page 8, that is the memorandum re liabilities, April 15, 1916. All the liabilities shown in this statement are either short date securities, one-year or two-year, or obligations current; and it is particularly to the latter that I now draw my hon. friend's attention. He will observe that apart from the London loans 10 p.m. and the Canadian loans, and the two-year and one-year notes, representing respectively $29,400,000, $16,200,000 and $14,000,000, there are the following items:
Bills payable-advances on construction of main line and branch
lines	 $ 7,300,000
Temporary loans cover-in? interest, construction, betterments and
equipment	$19,925,345
Less receivable from proceeds of securities, etc., applicable in reduction of the above.. 3,529,929	16,395,416
Then, on the top of the next page and embraced in the same statement, we have amounts owing to contractors, subcontrac-
., I J
tors, estimated, material accounts, etc., $5,912,407 and sundry accounts, capital account, coupon warrants, making an aggregate of $13,997,338. From this they deduct cash on hand, receivable, materials, supplies, etc., $10,780,389, leaving a balance of $3,216,940. Now, if my hon. friend will add together the $7,300,000 representing bills payable; the temporary loans less the amount receivable from proceeds of securities applicable in respect thereof, amounting to $16,395,416; the contractors estimates amounting to $5,912,407; and the balance of $3,216,940 in the last statement; he will find the immediate financial situation with which the Canadian Northern Railway system is confronted, aggregating $32,000,000. As T explained to the hon. member for South: Renfrew-and I filed a letter in connection, with this-the Canadian Northern Company have certified that, so far as the contractors' and subcontractors' estimates, monthly accounts, etc., were concerned, with the cash which remained on balance in the trust account and the financial resources which they had, apart from the $15,000,000, they would be able to meet that situation.
