TO' put the Canadian Northern in a position in which its current obligations would be taken care of, would require, not $15,000,000, but $24,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, the $10,000,000 does not enter. I am adding the $7,300,000 and the $16,395,416, making $24,000,000. That is the immediate financial situation with which, as I have stated, they are confronted. iMy hon. friend has asked me what are the details. So far as the $7,300,000 is concerned, that is perfectly clear, because that is represented by the balance payable by the company on account of the>
advances on construction of main line and branch lines. Then there are the temporary loans, aggregating $19,925,345-less receivable from the proceeds, $3,529,929; leaving $16,395,416-made up in this way: Construction

completion of main line and certain branches which were under construction, when war broke out, including interest on securities issued on same and ranking prior to the $45,000,000 guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, $14,612,477.51; less receivable from the proceeds of securities, etc., applicable in reduction of the above, $3,529,929; leaving a balance on that account of $11,082,548.51.

The construction of terminals, grade separation, Port Kells branch, and other capital expenditure, represent $1,846,867.49; and principal of equipment notes, $3,466,000, making a total of $16,395,416, as exhibited in these statements. My hon. friend asked what securities kvere in priority to the Dominion $45,000,000 securities.
I asked what was the amount of interest due.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In reality, all the securities of the Canadian Northern Railway system, with the exception of income convertible debenture stock, rank in priority to the securities of $45,000,000 which were issued under the Dominion guarantee by virtue of the legislation of 1914. I stated the other day that the entire fixed charges of the 'Canadian Northern system, which would include the interest upon the $45,000,000 were about $15,000,000 in round figures. I stated further that on July 1, by reason of the interest upon the $45,000,000 securities guaranteed, and upon the $35,000,000 securities, guaranteed undeT the legislation of 1911, which would be assumed by the Dominion Government for a period of three years, commencing this year, and by- reason of a similar agreement in British Columbia, under which the Government of that Province will pay interest for a period of three years upon the securities which it has guaranteed upon the Canadian Northern Pacific, the fixed charges, or net earnings of the Canadian Northern system would be reduced from $15,000,000 by the amount of $4,500,000. That is to say, for the coming year the fixed charge will be about $11,000,000, instead of $15,000,000, because the Dominion Government and the Government of British Columbia will be obliged to pay $4,500,000 in interest.
Do you defer these interest payments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The interest payments as theycome along will be taken care of by the company if they are able to take care of them; but I assume from the statement of estimated earnings, which I laid on the Table to-night, and which is certified by Mr. D. H. Hanna, the general manager of the system, that the railway company will be able to meet its fixed charges if there is taken into consideration the fact that the Dominion Government and the Government of British Columbia pay $4,500,000 a year for the next three years.
To come to the application of the $15,000,-
fSir Thomas White.]
000 which we are loaning to the Canadian Northern Company, I stated that it was the minimum amount. I pointed out the fact that there were $32,000,000 of immediate obligations, not funded at all, confronting the Canadian Northern Railway Company. There are two bearings to that. In the first place, the amount is exceedingly large, and they are unable to obtain more money because they have not the securities to pledge. Further, in the renewal of their notes, one year notes and two year notes, the question will at once arise when they come to renew these notes-and they must renew part of them this year-what about your unfunded debt, what about your immediate liabilities? The first question that is asked a railway company, or indeed any company, when it comes to put out an issue of securities, whether for long or short terms, is what is your financial position? The financial position of the Canadian Northern is that it has some $32,000,000 of liabilities. It is true that it has money in trust accounts and resources which will enable it to take care of the contractors' and subcontractors' estimates; but the remaining situation, some $24,000,000 or $25,000,000, is immediate, and consequently the $15,000,000 is, in my view, and in their view, and I think it will be in the view of any man looking fairly at this statement, the minimum amount with which they can hope to finance the company. It would take at least $25,000,000 instead of $15,000,000 to clear up these current obligations which they are not able to fund, and to replace which they are not able to effect new loans because they have no securities. We are not making them as large a loan as would completely restore their financial position. We are making them the loan of $15,000,000, and we say to them: " you have got to finance with that foT the coming year until we have this investigation and are able to look into the whole situation." They cannot get on with less than $15,000,000, and they have still this situation confronting them. I would like to say that the $15,000,000 which we propose to loan could be applied, under the terms of the estimate, in payment of any items to which I have referred, or partly so, namely, the temporary loans, covering interest, construction, betterments, and equipment, or to the liquidation of the balance payable in respect to advances or to the liquidation of the balance payable in respect of advances on construction on the main line and branch lines. We are not going to clear up the entire situation, but if we make them this

loan they will be able by renewing loans and replacing loans, having this situation in regard to current liabilities, to finance during the coming year. That is the position.
Does the minister propose to pay contractors who are indebted out of this money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The contractors who are unpaid will be paid by the Canadian Northern Railway out of moneys in trust against the $35,000,000 mortgage and the $45,000,000 mortgage to which I have referred. There is a credit balance at present to the account of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company $35,000,000 mortgage trust account of $1,301,719.70.
Why is that not used to pay these unfortunate contractors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just one moment, please. Then, in connection with the Canadian Northern $45,000,000 mortgage of 1914, there is a credit balance as of May 1, of $4,344,761. On the statement of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, corroborated by records in my own department, there is money lying to the credit of this trust account available for payment on construction account in accordance with the terms of these mortgages. My hon. friend from Calgary asks me why the Canadian Northern Railway does not pay the contractors. Personally I am not aware of the contractors being unpaid.
On the Canadian Northern Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not aware of it. This afternoon it was brought to my attention by a couple of sub-contractors, who said that they had not been paid by the principal contractors; but they were unable to tell me whether the Canadian Northern had paid the main contractors or not. But, as I had heard that there are accounts owing to contractors by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, I took the matter up in connection with this transaction with the Canadian Northern, and I am only repeating to my hon. friend from Calgary the assurance which has been given me, that out of the proceeds of these trust accounts and the available cash resources they would make payment of the indebtedness to the contractors. But it must be borne in mind that, although this money would be expended in that way, if there was a disputed account between a
contractor and the Canadian Northern Railway Company, they said that they would not necessarily pay the contractors the full amount that he claimed. It may well be that where they are in agreement they will say: "We owe you a certain amount, and we will pay you the amount that we admit we owe you;" but if there is a disputed account I do not think it is incumbent upon me to usurp the functions of the court and say: "You must pay the contractor the full amount .that he claims." If the claim is right they ought to pay it; but if there is a bona fide dispute the only way to settle it is to refer it to the arbitrament of the courts. But, in connection with this transaction which we are now considering, the Canadian Northern claim that they will be able to pay the contractors out of money and the proceeds of resources which they have available.

I would much rather they did the financing than I. With respect to the $15,000,000, as against $25,000,000, has the minister gone into the matter far enough to be able to say that the $15,000,000 will enable them to finance for the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be disposed to agree with my hon. friend, on the statement presented, that I would muoh rather they did the financing than myself; in fact, I indicated that in my speech of yesterday. At the same time they believe that if they get this loan of $15,000,000 to clear up their temporary obligations they will be able to renew their short date securities and finance during the year. It is upon that understanding that we are making the advance of $15,000,000. If it were not so we should either increase the amount or decline to make the loan. But they are satisfied that they can renew existing loans or make new loans, so that they can get the situation cleared up to the extent that we propose, but it does not by any means liquidate the temporary situation.

I notice on page 8, under the heading of " Canadian Northern Railway System," the audited statement of:
Bills payable-advance on construction of main line and branch lines, $7,300,000.
How far does that amount of $7,300,000 come into this transaction under consideration now, or does it come in at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might, because it represents indebtedness incurred on con-

struotioxi account. The Canadian Northern received advances with which it paid contractors who had done work upon the line or paid for material used in construction. They gave notes for that liability, but that money has all been paid to the contractors or for material, and the bills payable are outstanding and represent indebtedness.
What particular branch lines are those upon which this work was done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say offhand. I may be able to find out, but I would doubt it, because I should think these advances were made probably either last year, or a year and a half ago, probably since the 1914 legislation in respect to construction, some of the aocounts would be paid off, accounts would be adjusted from time to time, notes given and renewed or paid off, as the case might be. I doubt if it would be possible to say precisely with respect to what line the notes had been given, but I may be able to do it.

The point is that the loan going through now represents payment in some degree for work done on branch lines. It is not confined to the main line, as was the contention when the guarantee was going through two years ago. Therefore there is no question of principle that excludes from consideration the branch lines which they brought to the attention of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I assume that in the accounting the money might be applied to the indebtedness incurred by expenditures made upon branch lines, and in such case the mortgage is to cover not only the undertaking of the Canadian Northern but to further secure the amount expended upon the branch lines. But my hon. friend will not fail to gather this from the statement, or from what I have said, that in this particular case the money has been actually expended, and the Canadian Northern is confronted with the situation that it has these outstanding bills payable in respect to construction which has been done and which it has paid for by advances for which it has given promissory notes. I entirely followed what my hon. friend said a few moments ago, but I would point out to him that if the $15,000,000 is required by virtue of the present financial situation, then the Canadian Northern would not be able to build further branch lines, or to

make expenditures upon such branch lines, unless the Dominion Government gave a loan in excess of $15,000,000.

Quite so.
Sir "THOMAS WTHITE: We are not proposing to do that at the present time.

That is what we should
do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know
about that. There is nothing to hinder the Government or Legislature of Alberta tomorrow from giving further aid to secure the prompt building of these lines by way of subsidy or guarantee. The Dominion Government has this war on its hands, and the financing of this Dominion is about, the heaviest burden in this country to-day. Our banks are doing well, our financial institutions are in a stronger position than they have been for some years, the credit of the provinces is good, the credit of the municipalities is good; but the Dominion Government has to-day the burden of this war and will have it in the future. I do not say that we should not have the burden of the war; the burden of the war falls squarely where it ought to fall, that is to say, on the federal treasury.
But the point I am making is that if the construction of these roads is as urgent as my hon. friend has pointed out-and 1 believe he is right with regard to some of them-then it might be a proper thing for the Government of Alberta to come forward and, by granting subsidies or by giving additional securities, provide for completion of the lines. I have not answered my hon. friend, because I do not think it advisable to do so, with regard to a* matter of alleged collusion which prevented these lines from being built. To me there is a very simple explanation why the Canadian Northern railway has not built these lines up to the present time, although the monej to proceed with their construction lies, as stated by my hon. friend from Assiniboia, in the bank. The simplest explanation i? this financial statement that I have beer expounding to the House. In view of that statement, how could the Canadian Northern railway raise additional money for the purpose of constructing lines? And even if the money left lying in the bank were sufficient to construct the lines, would the *Canadian Northern railway, at this particular juncture in their affairs, confronted with the situation as disclosed by this balance sheet, be justified in starting these

lines knowing that, as soon as they were completed, the company would have the burden of carrying whatever deficit there was upon their operation, until such time as they became profitable.

Not starting lines, but
completing lines already started.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Even completing lines, and facing the deficit which they would have to meet upon them until they became profitable. I think with my hon. friend that it is very desirable that the sections he mentions should be reached. But railway companies, like individuals, have to do the best they can in the situation which confronts them, and the Canadian Northern railway, like the Grand Trunk Pacific, is to-day confronted with a situation in which they are not able to raise by the sale or pledge of securities the amount of money necessary to complete those lines. Nor aTe they able to face the financial situation which they would have to face by reason of the increase in their obligations due to deficits upon the operations of those lines. It seems to me that if the province of Alberta thinks it of great public interest that these lines should be completed, it might very well eo-me to the assistance of the Canadian Northern railway. As far as the Dominion 'Government is concerned, I think that at this juncture, considering the obligations devolving upon us and the immense burdens of this war, increasing as they are from day to day, we are bearing all the burdens for the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern Tailway that we .should be asked to bear. I believe these are the minimum amounts which will enable these two companies to continue solvent until we can deal in some permanent fashion with the railway situation.

I hope the minister will revise one phrase he used to-night. I understood him to say 'that although, the Canadian Northern railway had money in its treasury, raised on the credit of the province, it would not be warranted in spending that money in completing the bargain it had made with the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not say that. I proceeded upon the assumption that the money is not sufficient to build and equip the lines. What I was referring to was the additional amount the Canadian Northern will have to raise in order to complete the lines.
Mr.- OLIVER: I am very glad that the minister did not mean to convey the idea as I understood it, because it struck me as being a very serious statement for a Finance Minister to make. At any rate the position is this: He does justify the company in withholding from expenditure the money raised upon the credit of the province, when that expenditure is needed from every point of view.
I say that that is not a desirable position, and, sorry as I should be to criticise the Finance Minister, I certainly consider his attitude very seriously open to criticism. If I may be permitted to pursue this matter further, because it. is a matter of life and death to a portion of the constituency I represent, it is admitted that the Canadian Northern Railway has prosecuted work on some branch lines, and this Government is now prepared to meet the cost of that work without having had direction as to which lines the money should be expended upon. My hon. friend undertakes to draw the distinction between cases in which the company have already spent money, and cases in which the company is absolutely obligated to spend money in order to fulfil their agreements, On page 6 of the printed documents, I find in the list of securities of the Canadian Northern Railway system, under the heading " Guaranteed by Alberta Government," certain mortgage 'bonds and debenture stock of the Canadian Northwestern Railway-I think that means the Canadian Northern Western-showing an asset in the one case of $6,424,000, and in the other case of $2,799,997.73. If I understand this statement correctly, it is intended that a part of the $15,000,000 loan shall be used to pay the interest on these debentures. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of
this statement was to show the extent to which the Dominion and the provinces had given their guarantees. From the statement it would appear that the securities of the Canadian Northwestern Railway have been guaranteed by the province of Alberta and issued to the amount of $18,950,361.99-if the securities have 'been issued as stated, and I have no doubt they have. The interest would, of course, have to be paid, and to the extent that the Canadian Northern Railway was unable to pay that interest, it would be a charge ranking in priority, I think to the $45,000,000 mortgage, becauses my recollection is that under the legislation of 1914 the stock in this particular company is embraced in part of the mortgage premises.

As a matter of fact, we are going to vote money to pay the interest on the bonds of the Canadian Northern Western guaranteed by the provincial Government, the money realized from which is not being used to complete the roads. The roads are not completed and by reason of not being completed, are not in a position to earn the interest that would save its being paid by this Government. I think the case is clear beyond question. When this Government is paying the interest on money that was raised by that guarantee, surely, from the standpoint of the Minister of Finance himself, those roads should be completed and put in a position to earn interest, instead of this Parliament being compelled to pay that interest.

The position of the hon. member for Edmonton is most remarkable. He says that the Government of Alberta has guaranteed certain securities of the Canadian Northern Western railway, that the proceeds of those securities lie in the bank to the credit of the Provincial Treasurer of Alberta, that the company refuse to expend the money, and that the province of Alberta, unfortunately, is not in a position to compel the company to expend it. If that is the case, one of two things is the consequence: Either the province of Alberta made a very improvident bargain with the Canadian Northern, for which the Government of that province is responsible and should be castigated by the hon. member for Edmonton; or else it is impossible to do effective work with the proceeds of those securities; that is to say, it is impossible so to expend them as to make the road complete as to its expenditure. The hon. member for Edmonton must know that money can only be withdrawn from that account and expended provided the road advances to completion with each dollar of expenditure, at such a pace that it will be completed when all the money is gone. Consequently, unless the Canadian Northern Western has additional bonds sufficient to provide for the completion, mile by mile, there is no way by which the Canadian Northern Railway can get the money out.
Mr. OLIVER; Precisely.

Then I suppose the hon. gentleman is arguing that, wherever a province guarantees a certain amount, the Government of this country, if it protects the underlying security, that is guaranteed, must provide sufficient money to

complete the road. That would place the Dominion treasury at the mercy of a province. The province could give a small guarantee and then say to the Dominion Government: Now go ahead; we have already, by what we have done, obligated you to complete that road.
* Mr. OLIVER : Not at all.
Mr. MiEIGHEN: By our providing money to pay this underlying interest the province of Alberta is not providing it. The province of Alberta had control of the sale of the bonds. They should not have allowed the sale of the bonds until they knew that the company was in .a position to complete the road. If they find themselves responsible for interest in the meantime it is their folly, and it is to them the hon. gentleman should go with his castigation. Certain moneys were provided for certain definite purposes by the legislation of 1914. The purposes were all set out item by item -so much to such a road and so much to another; so much for improvements here, so much fox improvements there. Included in that were certain appropriations for the Canadian Northern Western, notwithstanding the fact that the Canadian Northern Western, at the request of the hon. member, remained a purely provincial road and outside the jurisdiction of this Parliament. If the hon. gentleman will look at the blue-book brought in 1914 at page 19, he will see that the proceeds of these securities were to go first in payment of contractors' liabilities in the Canadian Northern, and he will find that $1,809,000 for the Canadian Northern Western was included in the $21,000,000 of contractors' liabilities. And, if he turns to the book issued this session, at page 19, he will find that $1,809,697 of that $45,000,000 was to be applied to the discharge1 of these contractors' liabilities. At page 19 of the blue book of 1914 you find that $310,088 was the amount that was to be expended in new construction on the Canadian Northern Western. On turning to the blue book of this year we find that the following amounts were expended on that construction:	$140,042.47 and $174,444.53; total,
$314,486.90, or about $4,000 more than was contemplated to be spent in new construction out of the $45,000,000, in addition to discharging the contractors' liabilities against the road. Therefore, so far as the moneys under control of this Parliament are concerned, the Canadian Northern Western get the full benefit of the legisia-

tion of 1914; and if they have not received all that we undertook to do for them, if they still find themselves straitened, their money tied up, and unable to complete their lines, the fault lies at the door of the Government of Alberta, and there is where the hon. gentleman should go with his complaint.

I cannot follow the hon. gentleman's argument at all. He suggests that, according to my argument, the Government of Alberta, by guaranteeing the bonds of a railway, could obligate this Government to pay interest on the bonds. I said nothing so absurd, nothing could have been further from my ideas than what the hon. gentleman has seen fit to attribute to me. The Government of Alberta has guaranteed the bonds of other companies besides the Canadian Northern. It has guaranteed the bonds of the Great Waterways railway. There is no way by which this Government can be held responsible, directly or indirectly, for that provincial guarantee of bonds. But that is a different matter altogether from the Alberta Government's guarantee of the bonds of the Canadian Northern Railway upon lines which this Government took as a security for the guarantee given by it to the Canadian Northern, assuming proprietorship to the extent of actually paying the interest on the bonds. If this Government undertakes to pay the. interest on the bonds issued in respect of these partially-completed railroads, I say it is good business on the part of this Government to make such further arrangements, even if it involves the payment of money, as will secure the^ completion of these roads and put them on an earning basis, so that, instead of Parliament having * to pay interest, the traffic of the road will pay interest. That is my argument, and I am very sorry that I am not able to get the Government to see what I regard as an eminently fair and commonsense, as well as necessary, proposition.

A little while ago the Minister of Finance pointed out that the proceeds of the guarantee of 1914 had gone into the road. Has he any record or statement to show how much of the proceeds of that $45,000,000-some $36,000,000, I think-was paid to construction companies and sub-contractors that were owned and controlled by Mackenzie & Mann?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not aware of any. The Comptroller of the Railway
Department conducted an audit which, in my belief, was thorough, in which all vouchers were inspected and a complete examination made before these moneys were paid over. A more complete audit I could not imagine. His instructions were to see that the money was applied in strict accordance with the terms of the Act. Personally, I am perfectly satisfied that the proceeds of this $45,000,000 loan, paid over on the certificate of Major Bell, who is here to-night, and who did his work, in my judgment, most carefully and thoroughly, were properly paid out under the terms of the legislation of 1914 and the trust mortgage. It was pointed out in 1914 that Mackenzie & Mann were the contracting agents for the Canadian Northern, that they made contracts with sub-contractors and purphased materials, and they built the line; and it was the accounts of the sub-contractors and for the materials which went into the line that were audited by Major Bell. Major Bell tells me that in this matter he went below Mackenzie & Mann, acting as the construction department of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and inspected and audited the vouchers representing payments made to sub-contractors and for materials. Personally, I have not the slightest doubt that the money was properly applied.

That statement does not answer my question. All through the construction of the Canadian Northern from beginning to end this Government and the previous also, so far as I know, have handed over to Mackenzie and Mann, or the Canadian Northern Railway, millions, tens of millions, hundreds of millions of dollars by way of bonuses and guarantees, and no proper care has been taken to see that the money went into the railroads.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend say that this Government took no proper care in that respect?

Yes, that is exactly
what I say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What more proper care could have been taken than to provide by legislation that the money should be disposed of in a certain way and for certain specific purposes, and then to have a very competent official of the Railway Department audit and investigate all accounts and payments made before paying over the money? I have been familiar with the payment out of money on construction account for very many years in connection with business, and I do not

know any more strict system of supervision than is exercised by the Railway Department and the Finance Department in the payment of money under the provision of trust deeds securing mortgage issues of railway companies guaranteed by the Dominion Government. I have not the slightest hesitation in saying here to-night that I believe every cent of the money that was provided under the guarantee of 1911 under the late Government and of the $45,000,000 guaranteed under this Government has been properly applied for the purposes for which these moneys were designated by Parliament. The payment out of the money under the $45,000,000 mortgage has been precisely on the same principle as the money was paid out under the $35,000,000 mortgage for which my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew was responsible as Minister of Railways in the late Government.
I do not doubt it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will not be able to say that any different principle .has been applied, nor will the hon. member for South Renfrew, I am sure, admit that the provision which he made under the mortgage relating to the $35,000,000 guarantee upon the Canadian Northern Railway Company in 1911 was inadequate to protect the public which it was his duty to protect.

All I can say is this: That practically from the beginning to the end of the construction of the Canadian Northern railway the contractors for construction were Mackenzie and Mann, who let the work out to .sub-contractors. Is there any hon. member on either side of the House who does not believe that Mackenzie and Mann as contractors took many millions of dollars out of the moneys proceeding from the securities disposed of on account of the subsidies and guarantees by the provinces .and by the Dominion? If the money received from the securities issued on these railroads to the Canadian Northern Railway Company had all gone into the railroads, the company would not be here to-day asking for more aid, because the money would have completed the roads and put them in proper shape. My hon. friend talks about the wonderful audit made by the Railway Department. Well,
I am not much of a hand at auditing, but I notice that while the agreement was made in the middle of July, 1914, on September 12, less than a month afterwards,

a certificate was given for $12,500,000. I do not think that any audit worth talking about could have been made in that time of an expenditure of $12,500,000 in the construction of a railway. The certificates follow in order one after another, so that I do not pay very much attention to an office audit of that kind. It may be all right, but it is more likely to be all wrong. I understand that the proceeds of the $45,000,000 were only some $36,000,000. Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Here we have bonds guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada that are worth only a trifle over 80 cents on the dollar. There must be something wrong in that. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has been borrowing money at 5 per cen t. Of course, these bonds were at 4 per cent; that would make some difference. At all events, they realized a very poor percentage, and I think if we knew exactly what became of that $36,000,000 we would find that Mackenzie and Mann got a big percentage of it for their purposes. That has been their history from the beginning; to get guarantees and subsidies to build railroads. I will acknowledge that their main line is a pretty fair line.

What beginning does
the hon. gentleman refer to?
Although my hon. friend is a very young man, he is old enough to know when Mackenzie and Mann began to build railroads.

From the beginning to
the end,, that has been their practice; to get bonuses and guarantees and then issue, to any one who would purchase their bonds securities for a great deal more than ever went into the road. As I was about to say, the main line is not a bad road; I have been over it. But so far as the branch lines are concerned, I know that the proceeds of the bonds they sold, which were guaranteed by the provinces, let alone any other securities they issued on these roads, were far more than enough to build the class of road that they have built. Although they have milked the money out of these railroads and put it in outside private interests, when my hon. friend gave the guarantee of $45,000,000 in 1914 and took a mortgage, the outside securities were not put in at all. On that occasion the railway company ap-

peared to satisfy this Government that the $45,000,000 would see them through. That was the argument two years ago; what is the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and of the Solicitor General to-night? They bring down a statement and they show that $15,000,000 is the lowest amount that they can get through with. I think the Minister of Finance is right, because here is $92,000,000 of short date indebtedness. In the name of common sense, if this company is $92,000,000 behind, over and above all the securities that they have issued, what is the use of this Government pouring more money into it, especially when we do not know that all this money is going into the railroad? Although wre are responsible to-day for the $45,000,000 guarantee that was given two years ago, of which it is said that $36,000,000 has gone into the road, I doubt if more than $25,0000,000 has gone into the road.
My hon. friend comes forward to-day with a proposition to hand them out another $15,000,000. But if I understand anything about the figures put in our hands, that will not be all we will have to pay this year. Am I right in figuring from this point that in addition to this $15,000,000 we will have to pay interest on that $45,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, and upon
the $35,000,000 guarantee which my hon. friend voted for in 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

So that, in addition to
the $15,000,000 loan, we will have to pay the interest on the $80,000,000 guaranteed in 1911 and 1914, which will be about $3,000,000. So that this year we will have to pay out $15,000,000 plus $3,000,000, that is, $18,000,000 to the Canadian Northern Railway. We know where the $3,000,000 for interest will go of the $15,000,000; but we do not know where all of it will go. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance may be a clever man at handling money, and I give him credit for his ability; but I want to tell him he is not clever enough for the job he has in hand, to see that all that money goes through the hands of Mackenzie and Mann and gets to the right spot, and that none of it is diverted to their own purposes, on any of their side issues.
They will not get their hands on it.

If my hon. friend can do that and can show us that he has done so at the next session, I will give him more credit than I give him to-night, much as I respect his financial ability.
Where is this going to end? The company, according to their own showing, have $92,000,000 of present liabilities. And they are not satisfied with these present liabilities. These men are never satisfied unless they are branching out in all directions. During this session, as you know, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Blain), as chairman of the railway committee, we spent weeks and weeks up there fighting-why?	Because
11 p.m. this same railway company, in spite of their bankrupt condition, were bound to get their grip over the western part of Ontario and insisted on building lines there that the Government of the province of Ontario wanted to attend to. And their representative, I think the general manager and third vice-president, insisted that they had the money to build these roads. If they had the money to build these roads in Ontario that would cost tens of millions of dollars, why should they come to this Government and get $15,000,000 and $3,000,000 from the Prime Minister? That is something that has not been answered yet. There is something wrong somewhere, when they have millions of dollars to invest in Ontario, against the wishes of the people of Ontario to build roads which the people of Ontario want to build, and they have not a dollar to pay their debts, and they come to this Government to get this money, and this Government proposes to hand it over to them and get nothing at all for it. They are taking a mortgage. Well, I do not know what good a second, or third, or fourth, or fifth mortgage may be. I would not consider that that $15,000,000 mortgage, when it is completed and registered, would be worth $5. I would not give $5 for it, because in my time or in my children's time it will not be worth a $5 bill, with the interest.

The autograph
signature of William Mackenzie would be worth that.

That would be the only thing I would value the mortgage for, the autograph signature of William Mackenzie. I would not mind this so much if I could see any end to it; but just as long as this Government or any other Government of Canada will hand out money to Mackenzie & Mann every time they ask for it, so long will they come here demanding that money,

and you may as well face the music to-day as at any other time. My hon. "friend the Minister of Finance has told us what this war has cost us and what it is going to cost us, and we all know that this war will last for some time. Will we be in a better position to deal with this matter a year from now, or two years from now, than we are to-day, after handing over this money and thus adding to the road's liabilities and not adding much to its value? To my mind it is a case that calls for courage and skillful handling; and you are not going to better the condition by putting off the evil day. If I thought so I would offer no objection to this loan. But it seems to me that we are just going deeper and deeper into the mud, and we shall ultimately have to take the road over; -there is no question about that. I venture the assertion that the statement presented to us does not begin to represent the condition of the road, and that if this road should go into the hands of a receiver, and the receiver's auditors went through the company's books and found out the exact position of the road, a very different state of affairs would be disclosed. That is the objection I make to pouring this money into the pockets of the road when we do not know anything, or at least very little, about its true condition. An hon. member asked where we would be in the course of a few years if things took a turn for the good. We might get our money back. In the meantime the Government -has 40 per cent of the common stock of the. road, and I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and the Solicitor General that on this occasion, when we are coming to the rescue of the Government-
It is scarcely that.

Almost that, for in my judgment the Government is in just about as precarious a position as the Canadian Northern Railway is in. I meant to say that now that the Government is coming to the rescue of the Canadian Northern Railway, I ask the ministers if they are taking the precaution to make the Canadian Northern hand over their common stock-not that it is worth anything in the meantime in the way of cash value. But I ask if they are taking the precaution to make the road hand over a least a controlling interest in that common stock, so that when they come to deal with the road in the future, they will not be dictated to in the way the Canadian Northern is able to dictate to this or any other Government that may be in

power, under' present conditions. Now is the opportunity to do it. Is my hon. friend going to do anything of that kind? The Government can get that common stock if they insist on it. It is not, as I said, worth anything in cash to-day, but it would give the Government of Canada, after putting up this extra $15,000,000, control of the road whenever they wanted to take it, and it might save a .great deal of trouble in the very near future If $92,000,000 of debt is standing against the road, short date debts, and the company ran behind to the extent of $10,000,000 last year-

- if the company ran behind to that extent last year, when we had a most phenomenal crop, and when the Canadian Northern handled a very large percentage of that crop, how can the Government expect better things next year or the following year? It is altogether unlikely that we shall have such a crop as that of la-st year during the next five years. This year the acreage is very much less, and even supposing you were to have a yield-
The hon. gentleman forgets that last year, so far as the railway company is -concerned, ended dn June, 1915, and there could not be very much of the crop shipped at that time.

In that case they would not have the benefit of the large -crop, and that benefit will come within the present financial year. But I think I heard the Minister of Finance give an estimate which' did not show that the company were likely to be in a very fine position even with the handling of that crop. I asked the Minister of Finance yesterday if he could give any information as to what it would cost to complete the road, that is to- put the branch lines in shape so that they could do business profitably. Many of the branch lines cannot do business in the winter time, and cannot earn profits in the condition in which they are. A railway company cannot make profits on a road that is tied up by snow and frost for weeks and months at a time. I agree with -what my hon. friend from Edmonton has said. I will not speak for many of the provinces .except Saskatchewan, but I venture the assertion that there is not a branch line of the Canadian Northern in Saskatchewan which, if completed, and put in anything like decent shape, w-ill not earn operating expenses and

interest on the cost of the road-I will not say interest on the securities that have been issued against the road, but interest on every dollaT that went into the building and equipment of the road.
Why do the Grand Trunk branch lines not pay interest?
I think that their branch lines in Saskatchewan will pay interest.
Not one of them.
They will earn operating expenses and interest.
Only two of them earn operating expenses the rest show a deficit in that respect, and not one of them pays interest.

My hon. friend is probably taking only what the branch line itself earns, but he probably knows enough about railway matters, since he has- been a pupil of the Canadian Northern for two or three years, to know that a branch line is entitled to a certain amount more than is earned on the line itself, because it supplies traffic to the main line.
Then how is it that the main line is losing and is not paying operating expenses?
The Grand Trunk Pacific statement shows earnings amounting to $600,000.

On one part. But there is a deficit on the other part, and there is a net deficit of $200,000, or a deficit of $500 a day for every day of operation, without a cent for interest. I am taking it altogether. Even on the prairie division the earnings are a small fraction.
$600,000 is not a small fraction.
It is a very small fraction of the debt. Will the hon. gentleman fit that into his argument?

There is not branch of the Canadian Northern railway in the province of Saskatchewan that I have been over, and I have been over a great many, that will not earn operating expenses and interest, and that will not earn interest on every dollar that went into the building of the road. I do not say that they will earn interest on all the securities that are charged up against them, because when you charge up $20,000 of securities a mile
on branch lines on the prairie and you only put in from $10,000 to $12,000, or perhaps $15,000 a mile-
In the case of the Grand Trunk it is $42,000 a mile.

That may be, but the branch lines of the Grand Trunk are very different from the branch lines of the Canadian Northern. In most cases the Canadian Northern branch lines are very cheaply built, and ' they are charged up with securities to the extent of from $20,000 to $25,000 a mile.
Not quite.

Yes, $20,000 a mile. There was a railroad built by the city of Winnipeg from Winnipeg east within the last couple of years, and the only difference between the construction of that road and the construction of the branch lines on the prairie by the Canadian Northern is that the rails are somewhat lighter. They have a 60-pound rail, and in some cases the branch lines may have rails over 60 pounds. That road was built and equipped, as far as was necessary, for $12,000 a mile, or about half of what is charged up on the Canadian Northern, proving what I say that the money that this Government and the local Governments have advanced, as well as the proceeds of securities not guaranteed by either, has been switched from the Canadian Northern altogether, and put into concerns in Mexico, Toronto and elsewhere, and has gone into the pockets of the promoters of these enterprises. Now they come forward, and they do not put up one cent of their money. They did not put up anything two years ago when they came and asked for a guarantee. The Government gave that guarantee, and took no precautions to see that the money all went into the road, and now the company comes forward again and says: You must give us more money or we will throw the road on your hands. They came and held the Government up, and now the Government says: Well, we will give you $15,000,000 more and pay $3,000,000 of interest. That is the position of affairs to-day, and next year it will be just as bad, and perhaps worse. What are you going to do about it? Why not face the music like men? The war is not going to be over next year; certainly our war expenditure will not be over, and what better position can we expect to be in? We will have $300,000,000 or perhaps $400,000,000 more of debt than we have to-day, and we will be

These two railroads will have to be looked after in some way, and if the Government takes them over, or keeps on fathering them, we will be liable for the whole business; and we will have from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000 of fixed charges and interest to pay every year. The situation will be worse if you let Mackenzie & Mann handle the Canadian Northern. If you are going to give them the money, why not give it iri such a manner that you will have some control. I do not like the idea of Government ownership; I have no use for it if it can be avoided; but there may be a worse thing than Government ownership. According to my idea, -it is a worse thing to pour money in and let somebody else handle it just as it suits him while you take the liability, and while you are not sure that all the money goes into the road. That is the position we are in to-day, and I think the Government ought to reconsider their attitude in regard to the matter. There might be some excuse for going to the rescue of these two roads because the Dominion and the provinces have so much in them, but what excuse is there for voting millions, either money or guaranteed bonds, to take over two roads in Quebec and to add to the Intercolonial that is losing money every year, simply to help out a political friend at a time when Canada cannot afford to put $1,000,000, or $4,000,000, in cash or securities into these roads? It is bad enough to help out the roads that the Government has some liability for, but to shoulder new liabilities where the Government has no responsibility whatever is one of the most criminal things that a government could do considering the financial position that Canada is in to-day.
